messages.body_plain:
Hi, I don't know if anybody has already explored this idea, but the
following small modification of your code avoids exponentiation of log
likelihood:

waic <- function (stanfit){
   log_sum_exp <- function(x) {
     x_max <- max(x)
     x_max + log(sum(exp(x - x_max)))
   }

   log_lik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
   summands <- apply(log_lik, 2, log_sum_exp)
   correc <- - ncol(log_lik) * log(nrow(log_lik))
   lppd <- sum(summands) + correc
   p_waic_1 <- 2 * (sum(summands - colMeans(log_lik)) + correc)
   p_waic_2 <- sum (colVars(log_lik))
   waic_2 <- -2*lppd + 2*p_waic_2
   return (list (waic=waic_2, p_waic=p_waic_2, lppd=lppd,
p_waic_1=p_waic_1))
}

There was almost no difference in your example though:

messages.body_plain:
The autocorrelation time of the parameters that end up in my final chain object is very close to 1 for all parameters. So I certainly am taking way (!) too many samples.

Some of the reasons I was doing so many samples:
1) computing is relatively cheap. By submitting embarrassingly parallel jobs, 500,000 samples still only takes ~10 minutes walltime.
2) I wanted to make 'triangle' posterior plots with very smooth contours. I could probably do a kernel density estimate to get the contours, but again, it's cheap (in time and resources, except memory) for me to just run a ton of samples.
3) Testing had indicated there were differences in the maximum likelihood estimate between different runs, and so I kept ramping up the number of samples until the maximum likelihood estimate was relatively stable across different runs. This hasn't been properly tested, but I am moving away from AIC anyway (hence my interest in WAIC).

My goal wasn't necessarily to have you help diagnose and improve my method (though I certainly appreciate the comments), it was mainly to raise the question "how many samples is necessary for WAIC?" My general point was that if you want to use the AIC with MCMC samples, you have to get a good estimate of the maximum likelihood, which seems to quite obviously require alot more samples than the posterior statistics needed for WAIC. Maybe this is a blatantly obvious point, and I'm just overstating it.

To make decisions about the number of samples needed for WAIC, can one simply propagate the error of the mean and error of the variance (meaning for lppd and pwaic2) into a statistical error on WAIC, and use that as a metric? Is there anything fundamentally wrong with this idea, or is there a better approach?

messages.subject: PyStan on Windows
messages.body_plain:
PyStan 2.2.0.0 now works on Windows.

You'll need to be using Anaconda's Python 2.7 and Microsoft Visual Studio 2008
compiler (available for free download as Visual Studio 2008 Express).

Full instructions available in PyStan's documentation:

http://pystan.readthedocs.org/en/latest/windows.html

As always, feedback is welcome: https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan/issues

Best wishes,

-a

> Error : Error during user-specified initialization:
> mismatch in number dimensions declared and found in context; processing stage=initialization; variable name=alpha_phi; dims declared=(1); dims found=()
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
>

By dims declared=(1); dims found=(), it is saying that it expected alpha_phi to be a vector of length number of subjects but got a scalar.

> Neither does getting rid of init in the stan() function does not solve the problem. Not doing so results in:
> Invalid value of lambda: Error in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: lambda[k0__] is 18.190631465656615:0, but must be less than or equal to 10Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

All of these rejections are due to the fact that the constraints on the parameters and the constraints on the transformed parameters are not compatible. If lambda is a transformed parameter that must be <= 10, then whatever parameter(s) get transformed into lambda have to be constrained to make that happen. For example, if the parameter were lambda_squared, then it would need to be constrained to be <= 100.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On May 1, 2014, at 8:35 PM, Marco Inacio <marcoig...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi, I don't know if anybody has already explored this idea, but the following small modification of your code avoids exponentiation of log likelihood:
>
> waic <- function (stanfit){
>  log_sum_exp <- function(x) {
>    x_max <- max(x)
>    x_max + log(sum(exp(x - x_max)))
>  }

This is an excellent function to avoid overflow when doing addition
on the log scale.  Algebraically,

  log(a + b) -> log_sum_exp(log(a), log(b))

  log(a * b) -> log(a) + log(b)

It avoid overflow in exp() because x - x_max <= 0.

- Bob

Hi,
I had answered this, but my answer did not appear here due to a problem with using @aalto.fi <http://aalto.fi> email address for Google services, which should be fixed now.
Here's the answer again.

Yes, you can use usual approach for estimating the Monte Carlo error. It is quite easy to get this error small. Usually most of the uncertainty in WAIC (and AIC, DIC, CV, etc.) is due to not knowing the true future data distribution. See Vehtari, and Ojanen (2012). A survey of Bayesian predictive methods for model assessment, selection and comparison. Statistics Surveys, 6:142-228 http://dx.doi.org/10.1214/12-SS102 for further discussion.

Aki

I should have been more specific.  This is in RStan.  The model compiles
and then gives me a message about not accepting missing values.  I still
get the same message when I recode all of the NAs to NaNs.

I can work around the problem by just sticking in a highly unusual value
(I'm using 9999 when the units should be log(seconds)).  But this makes
it harder to check for illegal access to the missing values.

I think what I really want is a way to suppress the NA check when loading
data and just let Stan generate a runtime error (or return NaNs) if I accidentally
access the out of bounds data.  It would make me feel more secure.

  --Russell

Sorry to be confusing.  Here's the issue I created for RStan:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/67

and for Stan C++ (which will fix the problem in CmdStan):

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/637

There's actually nothing conceptually difficult about our accepting
all the valid IEEE floating-point values (finite values, NaN, +inf, -inf).

I didn't know what the Python status was, so I didn't create an issue.

> I can work around the problem by just sticking in a highly unusual value
> (I'm using 9999 when the units should be log(seconds)).  But this makes
> it harder to check for illegal access to the missing values.

Right --- not a strategy we want to promote long term, but it's what
we've been doing ourselves in some cases.  The problem is that NaN also
isn't a good distinguished code point.

It really will be better to just reformulate the data/parameters for
Stan if possible.

> I think what I really want is a way to suppress the NA check when loading
> data

I'm not sure what the NA check is, but if RStan looks for NA values and
gripes, that's the right behavior --- there's no way for us to get an
NA into Stan.  We can deal with NaN and +/- inf, but not NA.   And I don't
want to just convert NA to NaN, at least not by default.

> and just let Stan generate a runtime error (or return NaNs) if I accidentally
> access the out of bounds data.  It would make me feel more secure.

Not sure what you mean here.  You mean convert the NA to NaN?  I'd rather
see users do that explicitly on the outside from R.  R's the only platform
that has the special NA value.  It's not something we plan to support inside
of Stan.

Hello all,

I recently installed rstan on a new machine and encountered a mysterious "expectation failure" error, which can be reproduced as follows:

> oxford <- stan_demo("oxford")
> "K" <-
+ 120
> "r1" <-
+ c(3, 5, 2, 7, 7, 2, 5, 3, 5, 11, 6, 6, 11, 4, 4, 2, 8, 8, 6,
+ 5, 15, 4, 9, 9, 4, 12, 8, 8, 6, 8, 12, 4, 7, 16, 12, 9, 4, 7,
.... [TRUNCATED]
> "n1" <-
+ c(28, 21, 32, 35, 35, 38, 30, 43, 49, 53, 31, 35, 46, 53, 61,
+ 40, 29, 44, 52, 55, 61, 31, 48, 44, 42, 53, 56, 71, 43, 43, 43,  .... [TRUNCATED]

> "r0" <-
+ c(0, 2, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 4, 2, 1, 7, 4, 3, 5, 3, 2,
+ 4, 1, 4, 5, 2, 7, 5, 8, 2, 3, 5, 4, 1, 6, 5, 11, 5, 2, 5, 8,
 .... [TRUNCATED]

> "n0" <-
+ c(28, 21, 32, 35, 35, 38, 30, 43, 49, 53, 31, 35, 46, 53, 61,
+ 40, 29, 44, 52, 55, 61, 31, 48, 44, 42, 53, 56, 71, 43, 43, 43,  .... [TRUNCATED]

> "year" <-
+ c(-10, -9, -9, -8, -8, -8, -7, -7, -7, -7, -6, -6, -6, -6, -6,
+ -5, -5, -5, -5, -5, -5, -4, -4, -4, -4, -4, -4, -4, -3, -3, - .... [TRUNCATED]

TRANSLATING MODEL 'oxford' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
  failed to parse Stan model 'oxford' with error message:
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=38, column=2

}
 ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Parser expecting: <model declaration>

Any thoughts on what might be going on? I am using rstan Version 2.2.0 and R version 3.1.0 on Mac OS X 10.9.2. Thanks for your help!

Devin

On Monday, May 5, 2014 5:39:30 PM UTC-4, Devin Caughey wrote:
> I recently installed rstan on a new machine and encountered a mysterious "expectation failure" error, which can be reproduced as follows:

messages.subject: Re: NaNs and Ragged Arrays
messages.body_plain:
Two thoughts:.

One, I tested in the R console and is.na <http://is.na>(NaN) returns TRUE.  I'm pretty sure that the same thing is true for the C function isNA.  This explains why the behaviour was the same for NA and NaN.

The second thought is that you might want an "allowNaN" flag to allow accepting non-finite values.  That way you get around people simply putting in NAs for missing data and assuming that Stan will magically impute without any kind of imputation model.

On Sunday, May 4, 2014 10:09:16 AM UTC-4, Russell Almond wrote:
> I have data which is related to a series of events (keystrokes) on a collection of individuals.  It is a ragged array as each individual has a different number of events.
>
> This is not too difficult to model as I simply put it in an array with rows representing individuals and columns representing events and then fill the irrelevant parts with NAs.
>
> The relevant parts of my model are:
> Enter code here...data {
>
>   /* Fixed Structural Parameters */
>   int<lower=1> I;    //number of essays, index for essays
>   int<lower=1> J[I]; // number of events per essay,  index for events,
>   int<lower=1> Jmax;  //Jmax <- max(J);
>
>   ...
>
>   /* Data */
>   matrix[I,Jmax] Y;               // log pause time
> }
> parameters {...}
> model {
>   ...
>   /* Likelihood for data */
>   for (i in 1:I) {
>     for (j in 1:J[i]) {
>       ... // Do things with Y[i,j]
>     }
>   }
> }
>
>
>
>
> It shouldn't matter what I fill the values of Y[i,j] for j>J[i] with as these values are never scanned.  In R, I fill them with NAs, so if I accidentally reference one of those cells I'll get an error message or NAs all over indicating that I accidentally accessed an illegal value.  I would like to do the same thing in Stan.  I can understand why you don't want to deal with the overhead of R's NA handling, but it seems to me that IEEE NaNs would be perfect for the job and would not require any modification to the code.  (Yes, they might produce run time errors, but that would be fine).
>

messages.subject: Hard case for MRP
messages.body_plain:
This is more of a modeling question than a Stan question, but I was hoping that someone here would have some insight. If you know of a better forum for such questions, that would be useful too.

I'm working on a problem that at first seemed like a clear case where multilevel modeling would be useful, but as I've dug into it I've found that it doesn't quite fit the usual pattern because it seems to require a very difficult post-stratification. Here is the situation, simplified somewhat. You have a question in a survey, and you need to estimate the proportion of positive responses to the question for a large number (100) of different subgroups of the total population at which the survey is aimed. If these were disjoint subgroups then this would be a standard multi-level modeling problem, but they are not disjoint: each subgroup is defined by one or two variables, but there are a total of over 30 variables used to define subgroups. For example, if x[i], 1 <= i <= 30, are the variables used to define subgroups, subgroup i for i <= 30 might be defined as those individuals for which x[i] > 1, with the other subgroups involving combinations of two or possibly three variables. The interest in multilevel modeling comes from the fact that the sample size for a number of the subgroups can be fairly small.

You could do a multilevel regression with post-stratification, but that post-stratification step looks very difficult. It seems that you would need to model the 30-dimensional joint distribution for the 30 variables describing subgroups.

Has anyone here dealt with a problem like this before, or know of some relevant papers to read?

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Large number of errors when attempting to run code and I'm not sure what to do.
messages.body_plain:
In parameters, you have

real<lower=-.7> lluce[numberofsubjects];
real<lower=0> llambda[numberofsubjects];

while in transformed parameters, you have

real <lower=1, upper=10> lambda[numberofsubjects];
real <lower=0, upper=2>  luce[numberofsubjects];

luce[j]   <- exp(lluce[j]);
lambda[j] <- exp(llambda[j]);

How can luce[j] be guaranteed to be less than 2 if there is no upper bound on lluce[j] and how can lambda[j] be less than 10 if there is no upper bound on llambda[j]? That is what I mean by incoherent constraints. If you reconcile those, then you probably won't have to worry about getting the dimensions of the starting values right.

Ben

The above error message is telling you that the Stan model is not valid, thus it's not compiling. It's not compiling because the definition of matrix is expecting the number of rows and the number of columns within the square brackets. It should look something like:
   matrix[M, N] x;

This error message is also telling you that the Stan model isn't valid. The compiler is expecting square brackets with the declaration of the vector, not after the variable, which is creating an array. So it should look like:
  vector[N] x;

For more information, Bob has written a comprehensive section in the Stan manual called "Containers: Arrays, Vectors, and Matrices."

I believe a few messages ago, you got past this and were having issues with initial values, but it looks like you've changed your Stan model. My suggestion is to first create a working Stan model and see if it'll fit without initialization.

I'll stop here because it looks like Ben just responded and may provide more insightful information.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, May 6, 2014 12:36:29 AM UTC-4, Josh Rosenau wrote:
> Is this the right way to handle this issue? I’m testing it out and seeing if the results make sense, but I could see ways that this could be conceptually problematic, or at least inefficient. If there’s a better way, I’d love to know more. If I have to continue treating the two vectors separately, it’s not the end of the world either,  but the multi_normal approach would capture a meaningful covariance.

The general rule is that the support of the prior and the parameter (vector) should be the same. So, using a multi_normal distribution when one of the components is strictly positive yields a wrong posterior distribution. It is not so bad if the posterior distribution puts essentially no mass on the negative numbers for that component, but it is hard to know whether that would be the case in advance. In principle, you could get by with a truncated multivariate normal, but Stan doesn't support truncation for multivariate distributions.

I think you have two main options. The first would be to use a multivariate normal distribution for the log of the positive variable and the other variables. You could then antilog as necessary. The other approach would be to use some distribution for positive random variables for the first component and use a conditional multivariate normal for the rest.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hard case for MRP
messages.body_plain:
On May 6, 2014, at 3:45 AM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:

> This is more of a modeling question than a Stan question, but I was hoping that someone here would have some insight. If you know of a better forum for such questions, that would be useful too.

e-mail Andrew and he'll blog about it :-)   Otherwise, he might answer
here.  I don't have any experience with multilevel modeling with non-disjoint
subgroups.

- Bob

> I'm working on a problem that at first seemed like a clear case where multilevel modeling would be useful, but as I've dug into it I've found that it doesn't quite fit the usual pattern because it seems to require a very difficult post-stratification. Here is the situation, simplified somewhat. You have a question in a survey, and you need to estimate the proportion of positive responses to the question for a large number (100) of different subgroups of the total population at which the survey is aimed. If these were disjoint subgroups then this would be a standard multi-level modeling problem, but they are not disjoint: each subgroup is defined by one or two variables, but there are a total of over 30 variables used to define subgroups. For example, if x[i], 1 <= i <= 30, are the variables used to define subgroups, subgroup i for i <= 30 might be defined as those individuals for which x[i] > 1, with the other subgroups involving combinations of two or possibly three variables. The interest in multilevel modeling comes from the fact that the sample size for a number of the subgroups can be fairly small.
>
> You could do a multilevel regression with post-stratification, but that post-stratification step looks very difficult. It seems that you would need to model the 30-dimensional joint distribution for the 30 variables describing subgroups.
>
> Has anyone here dealt with a problem like this before, or know of some relevant papers to read?

On May 6, 2014, at 12:40 AM, Russell Almond <alm...@acm.org> wrote:

> Two thoughts:.

Thanks for following up.  You've started a discussion on the dev side
about whether we want to support something like NA and I think the
jury's going to be out for a while on this one, because those of us
coming from a C++/programming background have a rather different view
on the matter than those of us coming from an R/stats background.
(Not saying one is right or wrong, just that we don't all agree on
whether NA is worth the hassle or not.)

>
> One, I tested in the R console and is.na <http://is.na>(NaN) returns TRUE.

I think this just shows how broken R's type system is!
is.nan(NA) is FALSE and is.nan(NaN) is TRUE, so why they decided
to treat NaN as a kind of NA is beyond me.

> I'm pretty sure that the same thing is true for the C function isNA.  This explains why the behaviour was the same for NA and NaN.

What C(++) function are you talking about?  There's no NA values
in C++, just IEEE arithmetic.

> The second thought is that you might want an "allowNaN" flag to allow accepting non-finite values.

I'm not sure what you're suggesting here in terms of values in
R and how they're rendered in Stan.  Stan simply doesn't have an
NA value (Ben suggested following Stata and reserving the largest
double values for special uses, but I'm still skeptical).

> That way you get around people simply putting in NAs for missing data and assuming that Stan will magically impute without any kind of imputation model.

I don't think we're going to go to any kind of non-explicit imputation scheme.

- Bob

On May 6, 2014, at 12:19 PM, Sean O'Riordain <seor...@tcd.ie> wrote:

> Bob,
> I'd vote for NAs.
>

You're not alone!

Lots of people like R's way of doing things, too.  But I find almost
every decision they made very confusing from a computer science perspective.
Python, on the other hand, does almost everything the way I would expect
a scripting language to behave.

> I think you might have things the wrong way around when you say
> "I think this just shows how broken R's type system is!
> is.nan(NA) is FALSE and is.nan(NaN) is TRUE, so why they decided
> to treat NaN as a kind of NA is beyond me."

Just to be perfectly clear, it's not the existence of NA that I
object to, but the *** line, which treats NaN as a kind of NA.

is.nan(NA)  : FALSE
is.nan(NaN) : TRUE

is.na <http://is.na>(NA)   : TRUE
is.na <http://is.na>(NaN)  : TRUE  ***

If you're going to have NA mean "undefined" and NaN mean ill-defined (i.e., 0/0
or 0 * infinity), you don't want to confuse them, no matter how they're represented
internally.

I find this kind of thing very very confusing:

> a = 0/0

> exists("a")
[1] TRUE

> is.na <http://is.na>(a)
[1] TRUE

You get the same thing if you just set a = NA, which is why it doesn't
feel to me like it's truly an "undefined" value, because that's not how
it behaves semantically.

> I could be mistaken, but it is my understanding that the original R authors chose a special value of an NaN as NA a long time ago so this is perfectly sensible.

People definitely have different opinions on these things.  As
you can see if you follow our recent stan-dev discussion.  No idea
what we'll do about it long term.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
init=0 initializes to zero on the unconstrained scale, so this is fine here.  Indeed, unless
you specify explicit initialization values for each parameter the initialization is always
done on the unconstrained scale.

The problem is in one these two lines,

>   delta  ~ student_t(4, d, sigma_delta);

>   delta_new ~ student_t(4, d, sigma_delta);

The value of sigma_delta is overflowing/underflowing and causing the call to student_t
to fail.  If this is happening rarely then there’s no problem as the failures are handled
appropriately by the Markov chain, but if it’s happening often (say, more than 10% of
iterations) then the model has some issues.

You’ll want to use the right initializations,
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/models/bugs_examples/vol1/blocker/blocker.init.R,
which give reasonable results.

If there's a better way, I'd love to know more. If I have to continue treating the two vectors separately, it's not the end of the world either,  but the multi_normal approach would capture a meaningful covariance.
> >>
> >> The general rule is that the support of the prior and the parameter (vector) should be the same. So, using a multi_normal distribution when one of the components is strictly positive yields a wrong posterior distribution. It is not so bad if the posterior distribution puts essentially no mass on the negative numbers for that component, but it is hard to know whether that would be the case in advance. In principle, you could get by with a truncated multivariate normal, but Stan doesn't support truncation for multivariate distributions.
> >>
> >> I think you have two main options. The first would be to use a multivariate normal distribution for the log of the positive variable and the other variables. You could then antilog as necessary. The other approach would be to use some distribution for positive random variables for the first component and use a conditional multivariate normal for the rest.

messages.subject: suggestion: monitor() speedup
messages.body_plain:
This email is just to capture a speedup suggestion for the rstan monitor() function.

For reasons previously discussed, I have switched to using plain Metropolis-Hastings MCMC written in R with an Rcpp inline likelihood function.  A simulation of 6 chains each of length 250,000 iterations (yes it is very slow to converge!) takes about 15 seconds.

However, when I pass the suitably formatted matrix into the rstan::monitor() function to analyse the results it takes about 30 minutes to produce the output - this seems a bit slow!

I recognise that this will not be a high priority given that rstan needs considerably fewer iterations to converge, but it is my understanding that you would like monitor() to be more generally used by those of us who are not able to use HMC?

Kind regards,

Sean O'Riordain
Trinity College,
Dublin

> It varies. Sometime one chain has one error while sometimes two or three chains have errors.

That's fine.  Read the rest of the message.

It's an error being spit out by the student_t function, but not an
error for the sampler.  The sampler swallows the error from the
function, Metropolis rejects the proposal, and continues.  This doesn't
cause a problem in the posterior unless it's happening very frequently.
If it does happen very frequently, it can indicate a problem in the model
specification, which is why we're dumping the message out.

But I really think we need to just eliminate it or make it optional,
or figure out how to get rid of the word "error", because a large
segment of our user population focuses on the fact that something's
getting spit out and thinks Stan or their model is broken.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
We have different expertises.  Ben's the expert on multivariate
modeling, linear algebra, and in general on stat modeling issues.
I think he knows more about obscure (some may say "general") distributions
than the rest of us put together.  He's the one who came up with the
LKJ distributions for Stan.

I'm the one who built the parser for the language and designed most
of it and most of the code generation (with help, of course --- Marcus
and Daniel have also touched the code, but I think everyone else runs
screaming from the parser).

Marcus wrote the optimizers for point estimates, and also rewrote our
core auto-diff for linear algebra, which gave us a huge speedup.

Daniel's done all the testing and make, as well as writing our error
handling functions and a lot of the code for everything from R-hat
to effective sample sizes.  Daniel and I handle the template metaprogramming.

Michael's the geometry expert and expert in HMC (and other sampler
behavior).  He's also just insanely good at math.  Michael also
wrote the CmdStan command framework (perhaps why it's both
so cool and so non-standard for commands).

Daniel and I are usually the first responders to generic messages
because we're the only two project members being supported to work
on Stan full time and we want to save everyone else's effort for
where it's really needed.  Michael's also very active on the list,
and Ben when he's not knee deep in teaching and other projects.

Jiqiang wrote and maintains RStan and Allen wrote and maintains PyStan.

Matt, who's not really active in development any more, but occasionally
joins in on design issues and who we occassionally tap for his deep
algorithm expertise.  He wrote NUTS and with me, wrote the very first
prototype for Stan.

Peter Li's our amazing undergrad, who's coming back this summer.
He wrote a ton of code --- almost all of the forward auto-diff and
all of the random-number generators.

- Bob

>
> On May 6, 2014, at 2:22 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > Ignore my last comment.  In general, always listen to Ben :-)
> >
> > The way you put together the compound eta is right, but you can't
> > then sample with variable parameters because it doesn't normalize
> > the truncation properly.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > On May 6, 2014, at 7:15 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >> On Tuesday, May 6, 2014 12:36:29 AM UTC-4, Josh Rosenau wrote:
> >> Is this the right way to handle this issue? I'm testing it out and seeing if the results make sense, but I could see ways that this could be conceptually problematic, or at least inefficient. If there's a better way, I'd love to know more. If I have to continue treating the two vectors separately, it's not the end of the world either,  but the multi_normal approach would capture a meaningful covariance.
> >>
> >> The general rule is that the support of the prior and the parameter (vector) should be the same. So, using a multi_normal distribution when one of the components is strictly positive yields a wrong posterior distribution. It is not so bad if the posterior distribution puts essentially no mass on the negative numbers for that component, but it is hard to know whether that would be the case in advance. In principle, you could get by with a truncated multivariate normal, but Stan doesn't support truncation for multivariate distributions.
> >>
> >> I think you have two main options. The first would be to use a multivariate normal distribution for the log of the positive variable and the other variables. You could then antilog as necessary. The other approach would be to use some distribution for positive random variables for the first component and use a conditional multivariate normal for the rest.
> >>
> >> Ben

messages.subject: seeds & random number streams
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Just a quick question concerning seeds (the manual was not too precise on that): In case I want to start multiple chains in parallel for my stan model, then I would do this:

./model init=0 seed=1234 id=1
./model init=0 seed=1234 id=2

Now all chains would start from the very same initial value *and* seed. However, does Stan use the id in order to make the random number generator streams independent? This is what I assumed all the time, but I was looking for a statement like this in the manual and could not find it.

Many thanks for clarification!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] seeds & random number streams
messages.body_plain:
Stan uses a L’ecuyer RNG and strides the chain RNGs using the a multiple of the chain ID.

On May 7, 2014, at 3:53 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> What does that mean? Is the "true" seed something like seed + id. I mean how does stan create independent random number streams from a seed and an id? I know how this work for L'ecuyer (or however it is spelled), but what is the stan way to do that?
>
> This could be a bit more explicit in the manual (or I overlooked), but from quick going trough it, I only found that the id is a magic process id.
>
> On Wednesday, May 7, 2014 4:42:01 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > Yes, the seed gets advanced by the chain id so those two chains would
> > indeed produce independent chains.
> >

> > > Hi!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] error message: Error in function stan::prob::student_t_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter is 1.
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] error message: Error in function stan::prob::student_t_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter is 1.
messages.body_plain:
The relevant ratio is not messages / per chain but message / iteration.  If every
transition of the Markov chain rejects because of this problem you have a bad
model, if only a few transitions are rejected because of it then you’re okay.

On May 7, 2014, at 3:59 PM, Yingjie Hu <bynbut...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thank you, Bob.
>
> What is the definition of "sporadically“? Can it be called "sporadically“ that every chain has one informational message?
>
> On Wednesday, May 7, 2014 5:08:57 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > On May 7, 2014, at 5:19 AM, Yingjie Hu <bynbut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > It varies. Sometime one chain has one error while sometimes two or three chains have errors.
> >
> > That's fine.  Read the rest of the message.
> >
> > It's an error being spit out by the student_t function, but not an
> > error for the sampler.  The sampler swallows the error from the
> > function, Metropolis rejects the proposal, and continues.  This doesn't
> > cause a problem in the posterior unless it's happening very frequently.
> > If it does happen very frequently, it can indicate a problem in the model
> > specification, which is why we're dumping the message out.
> >
> > But I really think we need to just eliminate it or make it optional,
> > or figure out how to get rid of the word "error", because a large
> > segment of our user population focuses on the fact that something's
> > getting spit out and thinks Stan or their model is broken.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> >
> > >
> > > Why did you think it is not an error? I thought it was an error because it said "Error in function stan::prob::student_t_log".
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, May 6, 2014 6:58:45 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > But does it happen intermittently (and only during warmup) or does it
> > > happen at every iteration?  It’s only a warning not an error.

> > >> code <- '
> > >> data {
> > >>   int<lower=0> N;
> > >>   int<lower=0> nt[N];
> > >>   int<lower=0> rt[N];
> > >>   int<lower=0> nc[N];
> > >>   int<lower=0> rc[N];
> > >> }
> > >> parameters {
> > >>   real d;
> > >>   real<lower=0> sigmasq_delta;
> > >>   vector[N] mu;
> > >>   vector[N] delta;
> > >>   real delta_new;
> > >> }
> > >> transformed parameters {
> > >>   real<lower=0> sigma_delta;
> > >>   sigma_delta <- sqrt(sigmasq_delta);
> > >> }
> > >> model {

> > >>   rc ~ binomial_logit(nc, mu);
> > >>   delta  ~ student_t(4, d, sigma_delta);
> > >>   mu ~ normal(0, sqrt(1E5));
> > >>   d ~ normal(0, 1E3);
> > >>   sigmasq_delta ~ inv_gamma(1E-3, 1E-3);
> > >>   // FIXME: sample in generated quantities in later version
> > >>   delta_new ~ student_t(4, d, sigma_delta);
> > >> }'
> > >>
> > >> # data

> > >>>   vector[N] delta;
> > >>>   real delta_new;
> > >>> }

> > >>> }
> > >>> model {

> > >>>   delta  ~ student_t(4, d, sigma_delta);

> > >>>   d ~ normal(0, 1E3);
> > >>>   sigmasq_delta ~ inv_gamma(1E-3, 1E-3);
> > >>>   // FIXME: sample in generated quantities in later version

> > >>> }'
> > >>>
> > >>> # data
> > >>> data <- list(rt = c(3, 7, 5, 102, 28, 4, 98, 60, 25, 138, 64, 45, 9, 57, 25, 33, 28, 8, 6, 32, 27, 22),
> > >>>             nt = c(38, 114, 69, 1533, 355, 59, 945, 632, 278, 1916, 873, 263, 291, 858, 154, 207, 251, 151, 174, 209, 391, 680),
> > >>>             rc = c(3, 14, 11, 127, 27, 6, 152, 48, 37, 188, 52, 47, 16, 45, 31, 38, 12, 6, 3, 40, 43, 39),
> > >>>             nc = c(39, 116, 93, 1520, 365, 52, 939, 471, 282, 1921, 583, 266, 293, 883, 147, 213, 122, 154, 134, 218, 364, 674),
> > >>>             N = 22)
> > >>>
> > >>>
> > >>> fit <- stan(model_code = code, data = data, iter = 1000, chains = 4,ini=0, seed=30)
> > >>>

> > >>>
> > >>> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:

> We have different expertises.  Ben's the expert on multivariate
> modeling, linear algebra, and in general on stat modeling issues.
> I think he knows more about obscure (some may say "general") distributions
> than the rest of us put together.  He's the one who came up with the
> LKJ distributions for Stan.
>
> I'm the one who built the parser for the language and designed most
> of it and most of the code generation (with help, of course --- Marcus
> and Daniel have also touched the code, but I think everyone else runs
> screaming from the parser).
>
> Marcus wrote the optimizers for point estimates, and also rewrote our
> core auto-diff for linear algebra, which gave us a huge speedup.
>
> Daniel's done all the testing and make, as well as writing our error
> handling functions and a lot of the code for everything from R-hat
> to effective sample sizes.  Daniel and I handle the template metaprogramming.
>
> Michael's the geometry expert and expert in HMC (and other sampler
> behavior).  He's also just insanely good at math.  Michael also
> wrote the CmdStan command framework (perhaps why it's both
> so cool and so non-standard for commands).
>
> Daniel and I are usually the first responders to generic messages
> because we're the only two project members being supported to work
> on Stan full time and we want to save everyone else's effort for
> where it's really needed.  Michael's also very active on the list,
> and Ben when he's not knee deep in teaching and other projects.
>
> Jiqiang wrote and maintains RStan and Allen wrote and maintains PyStan.
>
> Matt, who's not really active in development any more, but occasionally
> joins in on design issues and who we occassionally tap for his deep
> algorithm expertise.  He wrote NUTS and with me, wrote the very first
> prototype for Stan.
>
> Peter Li's our amazing undergrad, who's coming back this summer.
> He wrote a ton of code --- almost all of the forward auto-diff and
> all of the random-number generators.
>
> - Bob

>

> > Thanks. “Always listen to Ben” has been my mantra as I’ve been learning Stan.
> >
> > On May 6, 2014, at 2:22 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Ignore my last comment.  In general, always listen to Ben :-)
> > >
> > > The way you put together the compound eta is right, but you can't
> > > then sample with variable parameters because it doesn't normalize
> > > the truncation properly.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > > On May 6, 2014, at 7:15 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > >> On Tuesday, May 6, 2014 12:36:29 AM UTC-4, Josh Rosenau wrote:
> > >> Is this the right way to handle this issue? I'm testing it out and seeing if the results make sense, but I could see ways that this could be conceptually problematic, or at least inefficient. If there's a better way, I'd love to know more. If I have to continue treating the two vectors separately, it's not the end of the world either,  but the multi_normal approach would capture a meaningful covariance.
> > >>
> > >> The general rule is that the support of the prior and the parameter (vector) should be the same. So, using a multi_normal distribution when one of the components is strictly positive yields a wrong posterior distribution. It is not so bad if the posterior distribution puts essentially no mass on the negative numbers for that component, but it is hard to know whether that would be the case in advance. In principle, you could get by with a truncated multivariate normal, but Stan doesn't support truncation for multivariate distributions.
> > >>
> > >> I think you have two main options. The first would be to use a multivariate normal distribution for the log of the positive variable and the other variables. You could then antilog as necessary. The other approach would be to use some distribution for positive random variables for the first component and use a conditional multivariate normal for the rest.
> > >>
> > >> Ben

I see --- that's just the log of the binomial pmf.
I tend to think of "log likelihood" as the piece of a model
that gives log p(data|parameters,constants).

>
> (it is on page 308 in manual)
>
> logit(theta)=beta0 (lod odds)
>
> replacing theta by beta0  gives the following
>
> log[ Binomial(n/N, beta0) ] = nbeta0 - N log(1+exp(beta0))

> Yes, p is p-values (theta).

>
>  multinomial logit coded directly in stan.

Do you mean binomial here?  For multinomial equivalent of logit,
you just want to use softmax explicitly.

I still don't quite understand what your intent is from the formulas
above.  They're not multinomial.

You can just use inv_logit(alpha) on the log odds alpha and then plug
that into the binomial if you want, but I'm somehow thinking that's
not what you're asking.

The other problem I see is this:

> transformed parameters {

> >  {

You can't just apply inv_logit to the individual arguments. I'm guessing
what you want here is (a) a simplex data type --- that's for vectors
that sum to 1, and then softmax to convert the logit-scaled probabilities
to a simplex.

On May 7, 2014, at 5:33 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

I only mention the blockcluster package to specify the source of our data, its functionality has nothing to do with the stan program. Sorry for not being more clear on this.

> Your problem is here:
>
> > model {
> >  int rclass[N,D];
> ...
> >      rclass[i,j] ~ categorical(pi[i]);
>
> You don't ever set rclass.  The default value is 0, and then
> that causes a problem because 0 is not an appropriate outcome
> for a categorical.
>

Right, we saw that with some print statements we had but removed before posting. We did try to limit / set the range with:

     int<lower=1, upper=K> rclass[N,D];
  int<lower=1, upper=L> cclass[N,D];

in the model block, but got the error:

     Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
       failed to parse Stan model 'my_code' with error message:
     EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=20, column=36

       int<lower=1,upper=K> rclass[N,D];
                                        ^-- here

     DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
     require unconstrained. found range constraint.
     Parser expecting: <eps>

However we may be setting rclass inappropriately. Is there another way to limit rclass range?

> It looks like what you're trying to do is sample from the
> categorical(pi[i]) and assign the result to rclass[i,j], which
> is NOT how Stan sampling statements work.  They just increment
> the log probability with the value of
>
>  log(Categorical(rclass[i,j] | pi[i]))

Yes, that is exactly what we are trying to do. I suspect our approach therefore is not correct. We would need to both set rclass (and cclass) appropriately and change our likelihood specification code, is that correct?

> which presupposes that rclass[i,j] is set to a valid value.
>
> Also, given that you have a parameter declaration
>
> >   simplex[L] pj[D];
>
> you almost certainly don't want to be doing this:
>
> >      cclass[i,j] ~ categorical(softmax(pj[j]));
>
> pj[j] is already declared to be a simplex, so it's already
> the right kind of thing to be a parameter to categorical().
> Now you're transforming it again by exponentiating the
> values in pj[j] and then normalizing.
>

Yes, absolutely correct. The "softmax" code was left over after some re-coding attempts and should have been removed before posting, sorry about that.

Thanks again Bob for looking at our code and your advice, its very much appreciated,
Joe

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] categorical distribution in mixture model issue
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] categorical distribution in mixture model issue
messages.body_plain:
On May 8, 2014, at 5:47 AM, Retzer Joe <retz...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Your problem is here:
>>
>>> model {
>>>  int rclass[N,D];
>> ...
>>>      rclass[i,j] ~ categorical(pi[i]);
>>
>> You don't ever set rclass.  The default value is 0, and then
>> that causes a problem because 0 is not an appropriate outcome
>> for a categorical.
>>
>
> Right, we saw that with some print statements we had but removed before posting. We did try to limit / set the range with:
>
>      int<lower=1, upper=K> rclass[N,D];
>   int<lower=1, upper=L> cclass[N,D];

The problem isn't not setting the bounds, the problem is that you're
trying to use "~" to do random number generation and assignment to
rclass, and that's not how Stan works.  It requires rclass and pi to
already be defined (not just declared as local variables) when you call
it.  The parameters are all defined by default externally by the sampler,
but any locals, transformed data, transformed parameters, and generated
quantities need to be set explicitly before being used.

>> It looks like what you're trying to do is sample from the
>> categorical(pi[i]) and assign the result to rclass[i,j], which
>> is NOT how Stan sampling statements work.  They just increment
>> the log probability with the value of
>>
>>  log(Categorical(rclass[i,j] | pi[i]))
>
>
> Yes, that is exactly what we are trying to do. I suspect our approach therefore is not correct. We would need to both set rclass (and cclass) appropriately and change our likelihood specification code, is that correct?
>

Correct.

What you really need to do is marginalize out any discrete
parameters.

- Bob

I'm assuming p is an estimated parameter, not literally
defined to be the empirical success rate.

I'd look elsewhere through the model to make sure you're
setting p to the right values and estimating it from the
right data.

Our general advice is to start with a very simple model and
build up --- it's much easier to diagnose problems when you
have a simple working model and the next richer model you want
to build that doesn't work --- it's easier to isolate what's
going wrong.

- Bob

On Monday, September 10, 2012 6:05:15 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Item-response theory (IRT) models are very much the kind
> of thing we had in mind when designing Stan -- it's essentially
> a logistic regression with high correlation among
> the parameters in the posterior.
>
> I just wrote four Stan models for the basic IRT
> models PL1 (aka Rasch) with no question discrimination
> parameter and PL2 with the discrimination parameter, along
> with multilevel variants of the kind described in Gelman
> and Hill's regression book starting on p. 314.
>
> You can browse the models online in our source repository:
>
> https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/#git%2Fsrc%2Fmodels%2Fmisc%2Firt
>
> I tested them by generating data for 400 students
> on 100 questions, with 25% of the data missing at
> random.  This results in around 30,000 data points
> and 500 (PL1) or 600 (PL2) parameters.
>
> The models take about 5 seconds to compile in g++ at -O3
> optimization.
>
> Here's how long Stan took to warmup for 500 iterations
> then sample for 500 iterations.  All models converged
> to appropriate answers across multiple chains.
>
>    PL1:  80 seconds (1m 20s)
>
>    PL2: 180 seconds (3m 00s)
>
> The hierarchical models took the same amount of time
> as their non-hierarchical counterparts.
>
> The PL2 models adapt to a smaller step size and more
> steps, which is why they take longer (that and having
> 20% more parameters and their attendant differentiation
> and updating).
>
> It only consumes 14MB of memory peak, so there's no
> problem running multiple processes concurrently.
>
> I also ran on much more data.  Basic IRT for 1000 students
> with 200 questions each (150K data points) ran
> 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations (twice as many
> as reported above) in 4 minutes in 70MB and converged to
> the right answer.  I even ran basic IRT for 10,000 students with 200
> questions each (1.5M data points), and though I lost
> patience testing, I extrapolated about 2 hours for
> 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations.  (I cut down
> the later tests when I realized it was converging very
> quickly from random inits.)
>
> There's a bit of variation in the runs mainly due to
> waiting for the step sizes to converge during warmup;
> if the random initialization is far from a mode, especially
> for the hierarchical parameters or intercept terms, then
> it can take a bit longer to move to the mode because of
> the need for reduced step sizes to keep the simulation
> accurate (I never saw more than about 50% more time needed
> than reported above).  With good inits it can run a bit faster than
> reported above.
>
> The notebook I tested this on is reasonably beefy:
>
>    Mac OS X, Mountain Lion,
>    2.3 GHz i7 CPU
>    1600MHz DDR3 memory
>
> Although I'm using the latest g++ from Xcode, version 4.21,
> the latest from Macports is faster (as much as 20% in
> some of our earlier tests of a version of 4.6 and they
> continue to get faster).
>
> - Bob
>
>
>

You mean in the results?  There's no way to save only a few, but there's
a way to extract only a few in RStan --- you just provide a second argument
to extract.

What information?  You can just pull the samples.

- Bob

>
> On Tuesday, May 6, 2014 12:35:17 AM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Hi Daniel,
>
> I think there's confusion between Stan's types and the R dump format's types. And these seem like different messages than what you've had before.
>
> Some insight into the error messages below:
>
> On Tue, May 6, 2014 at 12:23 AM, Daniel Berman <daniel....@gmail.com> wrote:
> When they are both matricies, i get:
> Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
>   failed to parse Stan model 'cpt_hierarchical_model_
> positive_and_negative24' with error message:
> EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=30, column=46
>
> 	matrix<lower=-3,upper=3>[
> numberofsubjects] alpha_phi;
>                                              ^-- here
>
>
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> Parser expecting: ","
>
>
> The above error message is telling you that the Stan model is not valid, thus it's not compiling. It's not compiling because the definition of matrix is expecting the number of rows and the number of columns within the square brackets. It should look something like:
>    matrix[M, N] x;
>
>
> when it's a vectors digit:

>

> Parser expecting: "["
>
>
>
> This error message is also telling you that the Stan model isn't valid. The compiler is expecting square brackets with the declaration of the vector, not after the variable, which is creating an array. So it should look like:
>   vector[N] x;
>
>
> For more information, Bob has written a comprehensive section in the Stan manual called "Containers: Arrays, Vectors, and Matrices."
>
>
> I believe a few messages ago, you got past this and were having issues with initial values, but it looks like you've changed your Stan model. My suggestion is to first create a working Stan model and see if it'll fit without initialization.

>
>
> Daniel

>
>
>
>
>

> Hi Daniel,
>
> Can you double-check the definition of alpha_phi and make sure it's a vector, not a matrix in your initialization file?

>
> Daniel

>

>
>
> real<lower=0> llambda[numberofsubjects];
>
>
>
>
>
> while in transformed parameters, you have

>
>

> I'm unsure how to address the first error. I've tried making the initial value for alpha_phi=rep(c(0),numberofsubjects), but that doesn't help. I would prefer not to change alpha_phi to a scalar because I hope to be able to run multiple data sets at the same time, meaning I would need multiple alpha_phis.
>
> Possibly it needs to be a one-column matrix?
>
> alpha_phi = matrix(0, numberofsubjects, 1)
>
> But the second problem with the model needs to be fixed regardless. It suggests the stated constraints are incoherent.
>
> Ben
>
>
> On Friday, May 2, 2014 9:28:23 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Friday, May 2, 2014 8:22:09 AM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
> Unfortunately declaring alpha_phi as an init doesn't solve the problem and results in the error:
> Error : Error during user-specified initialization:
> mismatch in number dimensions declared and found in context; processing stage=initialization; variable name=alpha_phi; dims declared=(1); dims found=()

>

messages.body_plain:
My data sets contain data points with negatives and zeros. Originally, I turned those into positives by multiplying them by -1, so I could put them to some power. I noticed that I was having some errors, so I printed out what was happening. I noticed that -0=-0, rather than 0 and (-0)^a resulted in an error.

When running R2Winbugs, you would run fit1=bugs(...), where fit1 is a list. After that you could use the command fit1$summary would return a matrix. When you use View(fit1$summary), the first row is row.names and contains the names of the parameters estimated. After that, the columns are titled with measures of the parameters such as mean, standard deviation, 2.5%, 25%, etc. This was easy to manipulate. Say I wanted the mean and standard deviation of the very first parameter, I would simply type fit1$summary[1,1:2] and it would return those as class numeric:

      mean         sd
0.69656000 0.09513074

Is there a way to do that?

messages.body_plain:
If you are using rstan you can use extract() to extract samples from a model

model1 <- stan(file="my_model.stan",  init =my.inits(), pars =my.params, data=my.data,  warmup = 200, iter= 2000, chains = 4)
output1 <- extract(model1, permuted = TRUE)

output1 will be an array and you can access the parameters by calling them by their name

output1$mean

or

output1$sd

the function print() will return you a table containing  a resume of the model

print(model1)

or if you want only to check one parameter:

print(model1, pars="mean", probs=c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975), digits=3)

Hope that help

Chris
-------------

messages.subject: inv_wishart_rng bug?
messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering whether there's a bug in inv_wishart_rng. I'm new to both Stan and inverse Wishart distributions, so could easily be mistaken. If there is a bug, does it also affect the other inverse wishart functions in Stan?

I tried sampling covariance matrices using inv_wishart_rng in Stan with RStan interface. With a 2 x 2 identity matrix as the scale matrix, and degrees of freedom 4, I was expecting that the mean of the samples would also be an identity matrix (e.g. p 574 in Bayesian Data Analysis, Gelman et al, 2nd edition). Instead, I get something in which the element [2,2] appears systematically larger than the element [1,1]. Also, from looking at the density function, it doesn't seem as though the support is only diagonal matrices if the scale matrix is diagonal, yet inv_wishart_rng only returns diagonal matrices.

I compared this to riwish() in MCMCpack, which seems to behave as I'd expect it to.

To see the difference, I drew ellipses of unit Mahalanobis distance around the origin for each sampled covariance matrix and their mean, for both inv_wishart_rng output and riwish output (invwishart.pdf, attached).

I'm using Stan 2.2.0, R 3.1.0, Rstan 2.0.1, MCMCpack 1.3-3, 64-bit Ubuntu 12.04, 16 G RAM. Session info and code attached. Not sure what C compiler R is using (but .R/Makevars also attached with session info, and I know I have g++ on my system).

On May 10, 2014, at 5:04 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I'm wondering whether there's a bug in inv_wishart_rng. I'm new to both Stan and inverse Wishart distributions, so could easily be mistaken. If there is a bug, does it also affect the other inverse wishart functions in Stan?

No --- they don't share any code.

> I tried sampling covariance matrices using inv_wishart_rng in Stan with RStan interface. With a 2 x 2 identity matrix as the scale matrix, and degrees of freedom 4, I was expecting that the mean of the samples would also be an identity matrix (e.g. p 574 in Bayesian Data Analysis, Gelman et al, 2nd edition). Instead, I get something in which the element [2,2] appears systematically larger than the element [1,1]. Also, from looking at the density function, it doesn't seem as though the support is only diagonal matrices if the scale matrix is diagonal, yet inv_wishart_rng only returns diagonal matrices.
>
> I compared this to riwish() in MCMCpack, which seems to behave as I'd expect it to.
>
> To see the difference, I drew ellipses of unit Mahalanobis distance around the origin for each sampled covariance matrix and their mean, for both inv_wishart_rng output and riwish output (invwishart.pdf, attached).
>
> I'm using Stan 2.2.0, R 3.1.0, Rstan 2.0.1, MCMCpack 1.3-3, 64-bit Ubuntu 12.04, 16 G RAM. Session info and code attached. Not sure what C compiler R is using (but .R/Makevars also attached with session info, and I know I have g++ on my system).

OK, that all sounds reasonable.  If the parameters symmetric in the two diagonal elements,
the output should be, too.

I'm opening a (high priority) issue:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/644

Thanks for reporting.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem resolving parameters using gaussian_dlm_obs
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the delay; end of semester cruch.

The problem was that the current implementation of the gaussian_dlm_obs only supports time-invariant DLMs (constant F, G, V and W), and in your model the regression values (F) are varying over time. The problem which allowed the model to be compiled in the first place instead of throwing an error is that the y argument to gaussian_dlm_obs should have dimensions (number of variables, number of observations), and you provided the transpose.  I hope to get to implementing a version of gaussian_dlm_obs with time varying parameters, but its not on the immediate future.  If the model is running too slow, the alternative is to implement the Kalman filter directly in Stan.

messages.body_snippet:
If you take:

  alpha <- alpha_raw * sigma_alpha + mu_alpha

and you need alpha > 0, this translates to:

and hence

> > On Monday, September 10, 2012 6:05:15 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Item-response theory (IRT) models are very much the kind
> > of thing we had in mind when designing Stan -- it's essentially
> > a logistic regression with high correlation among
> > the parameters in the posterior.
> >
> > I just wrote four Stan models for the basic IRT
> > models PL1 (aka Rasch) with no question discrimination
> > parameter and PL2 with the discrimination parameter, along
> > with multilevel variants of the kind described in Gelman
> > and Hill's regression book starting on p. 314.
> >
> > You can browse the models online in our source repository:
> >
> > https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/#git%2Fsrc%2Fmodels%2Fmisc%2Firt
> >
> > I tested them by generating data for 400 students
> > on 100 questions, with 25% of the data missing at
> > random.  This results in around 30,000 data points
> > and 500 (PL1) or 600 (PL2) parameters.
> >
> > The models take about 5 seconds to compile in g++ at -O3
> > optimization.
> >
> > Here's how long Stan took to warmup for 500 iterations
> > then sample for 500 iterations.  All models converged
> > to appropriate answers across multiple chains.
> >
> >    PL1:  80 seconds (1m 20s)
> >
> >    PL2: 180 seconds (3m 00s)
> >
> > The hierarchical models took the same amount of time
> > as their non-hierarchical counterparts.
> >
> > The PL2 models adapt to a smaller step size and more
> > steps, which is why they take longer (that and having
> > 20% more parameters and their attendant differentiation
> > and updating).
> >
> > It only consumes 14MB of memory peak, so there's no
> > problem running multiple processes concurrently.
> >
> > I also ran on much more data.  Basic IRT for 1000 students
> > with 200 questions each (150K data points) ran
> > 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations (twice as many
> > as reported above) in 4 minutes in 70MB and converged to
> > the right answer.  I even ran basic IRT for 10,000 students with 200
> > questions each (1.5M data points), and though I lost
> > patience testing, I extrapolated about 2 hours for
> > 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations.  (I cut down
> > the later tests when I realized it was converging very
> > quickly from random inits.)
> >
> > There's a bit of variation in the runs mainly due to
> > waiting for the step sizes to converge during warmup;
> > if the random initialization is far from a mode, especially
> > for the hierarchical parameters or intercept terms, then
> > it can take a bit longer to move to the mode because of
> > the need for reduced step sizes to keep the simulation
> > accurate (I never saw more than about 50% more time needed
> > than reported above).  With good inits it can run a bit faster than
> > reported above.
> >
> > The notebook I tested this on is reasonably beefy:
> >
> >    Mac OS X, Mountain Lion,
> >    2.3 GHz i7 CPU
> >    1600MHz DDR3 memory
> >
> > Although I'm using the latest g++ from Xcode, version 4.21,
> > the latest from Macports is faster (as much as 20% in
> > some of our earlier tests of a version of 4.6 and they
> > continue to get faster).
> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is there a voting page for requesting a new function?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is there a voting page for requesting a new function?
messages.body_plain:
On May 13, 2014, at 11:57 PM, Bero <heart...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> Is there a voting page for requesting a new function?  It will be useful information for developers' prioritization.

Not as such.  Feel free to comment here --- the developers
read these posts, or on the issue tracker, which is where
we keep track of feature requests.  Bigger things we keep design
docs on in the Wiki.

>
> I believe that many of the users want stan to have more usability and scalability,

Absolutely!  But then you have to say for which kinds of models.

> that is to say, discrete parameter and multi-threading, even if developers are not champions about them.

I think I can speak for all the developers in saying we are not
at all opposed to discrete parameters or multi-threaded evaluation,
it's just that we don't know how to implement them.  Having said that,
it's also not where we're putting our efforts, but I think that's
largely because we don't know how to.  Similarly, we've had requests
for map-reduce type implementations and for GPU-type implementations,
as well as multi-threaded implementations (for those not up on the various
ways to parallelize these days:  GPUs parallelize shared ops across
graphics processors, map-reduce more general operations across core processes --- usually across
machines on a  cluster, and multi-threaded implementations use multiple
cores on a single machine).

For discrete parameters, we can't just calculate the Markov blanket
use conditional sampling --- Stan's language doesn't define a graphical
model the same way a BUGS or JAGS model does.  We're very open to
suggestions on how we might do sampling.  We could take a very brute-force
approach and use the entire joint density/mass function and Bayes's law,
but it'd be very slow.

As to multi-threading, it'd be easy to do with a matrix library
that multi-threaded if you reimplemented all of Stan's underlying
data types, code generation, etc.  Or if Eigen, which is what we use
now, supported multi-threaded matrix evals.  At a higher level, we
don't know how to deal with multi-threaded evaluation in the face of
the need for automatic differentiation.

One place we might be able to multi-thread is with higher-order derivatives
like Hessians and with multivariate first-order Jacobians (though we rarely have to
explicitly compute Jacobians by auto-diff --- the place we will need to do it
is in stiff diff eq solving).

Our priorities for the immediate future are functions (due out in next
release), differential equation solvers (probably the release after that),
more efficient auto-diff and data types for higher-order models (coming in pieces,
starting in the next release).  We're also refactoring all of our interfaces
deeper into C++ to make it easier to support command-line, R and Python.
On the nearer, but not immediate term, we're going to introduce lots of point
estimation including EP, VB, and maximal marginal likelihood.  The plan is
to include data parallelization for EP and stochastic VB.

So it's not lack of interest --- we just have our hands full.  If people want
to volunteer, we're always looking for developers.  Especially if you can
figure out how to multi-threading and discrete sampling!

> For example, Supervised LDA and Relation Topic Model use the realized category indexes z instead of theta (topic distribution). Summing out doesn't work, right?

I'm pretty sure you could sum things out for supervised LDA of various
kinds, including that described by Blei and McAuliffe in the linked doc.

> http://people.ee.duke.edu/~lcarin/Iulian6.6.08.pdf

Observed categorical outputs are no problem.

I've built similar models for crowdsourcing (following Raykar et al.'s
JMLR paper) and for population models (following the CJS model with
predictors --- I didn't actually build this one, a user did).  In both
cases you get a mixed of observed and latent discrete parameters, the
latent ones of which can be marginalized out.

Not to say it's easy.  We'd much rather have the marginalization be
automatic and also to support explicit discrete parameters.

I don't know the relation topic model.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help with hierarchical negative binomial
messages.body_plain:
I don't know what's causing the compile error. But, one thing I saw on your model specification: you seem to be assuming that neg_binomial from Stan uses the parametrization of GLMs, that is, negBinomial(mean, overdispersion). But Stan doesn't, it uses a parametrization of Bayesian Data Analysis book, see the Stan manual.

R doesn't use it neither, it uses the simple parametrization that is taught in introductory undergraduate probability courses (see Wikipedia). To use the parametrization negBinomial(mean, overdispersion) in R, you must do:
rnbinom(100, 8, mu=9), where 100 is the number of draws to be generated, 8 is the overdispersion parameter and 9 is the mean.

>

> On May 13, 2014, at 11:57 PM, Bero <heart...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Hi,
> >
> > Is there a voting page for requesting a new function?  It will be useful information for developers' prioritization.
>
> Not as such.  Feel free to comment here --- the developers
> read these posts, or on the issue tracker, which is where
> we keep track of feature requests.  Bigger things we keep design
> docs on in the Wiki.
>
> >
> > I believe that many of the users want stan to have more usability and scalability,
>
> Absolutely!  But then you have to say for which kinds of models.
>
> > that is to say, discrete parameter and multi-threading, even if developers are not champions about them.
>
> I think I can speak for all the developers in saying we are not
> at all opposed to discrete parameters or multi-threaded evaluation,
> it's just that we don't know how to implement them.  Having said that,
> it's also not where we're putting our efforts, but I think that's
> largely because we don't know how to.  Similarly, we've had requests
> for map-reduce type implementations and for GPU-type implementations,
> as well as multi-threaded implementations (for those not up on the various
> ways to parallelize these days:  GPUs parallelize shared ops across
> graphics processors, map-reduce more general operations across core processes --- usually across
> machines on a  cluster, and multi-threaded implementations use multiple
> cores on a single machine).
>
> For discrete parameters, we can't just calculate the Markov blanket
> use conditional sampling --- Stan's language doesn't define a graphical
> model the same way a BUGS or JAGS model does.  We're very open to
> suggestions on how we might do sampling.  We could take a very brute-force
> approach and use the entire joint density/mass function and Bayes's law,
> but it'd be very slow.
>
> As to multi-threading, it'd be easy to do with a matrix library
> that multi-threaded if you reimplemented all of Stan's underlying
> data types, code generation, etc.  Or if Eigen, which is what we use
> now, supported multi-threaded matrix evals.  At a higher level, we
> don't know how to deal with multi-threaded evaluation in the face of
> the need for automatic differentiation.
>
> One place we might be able to multi-thread is with higher-order derivatives
> like Hessians and with multivariate first-order Jacobians (though we rarely have to
> explicitly compute Jacobians by auto-diff --- the place we will need to do it
> is in stiff diff eq solving).
>
> Our priorities for the immediate future are functions (due out in next
> release), differential equation solvers (probably the release after that),
> more efficient auto-diff and data types for higher-order models (coming in pieces,
> starting in the next release).  We're also refactoring all of our interfaces
> deeper into C++ to make it easier to support command-line, R and Python.
> On the nearer, but not immediate term, we're going to introduce lots of point
> estimation including EP, VB, and maximal marginal likelihood.  The plan is
> to include data parallelization for EP and stochastic VB.
>
> So it's not lack of interest --- we just have our hands full.  If people want
> to volunteer, we're always looking for developers.  Especially if you can
> figure out how to multi-threading and discrete sampling!
>
> > For example, Supervised LDA and Relation Topic Model use the realized category indexes z instead of theta (topic distribution). Summing out doesn't work, right?
>
> I'm pretty sure you could sum things out for supervised LDA of various
> kinds, including that described by Blei and McAuliffe in the linked doc.
>
> > http://people.ee.duke.edu/~lcarin/Iulian6.6.08.pdf
>
> Observed categorical outputs are no problem.
>
> I've built similar models for crowdsourcing (following Raykar et al.'s
> JMLR paper) and for population models (following the CJS model with
> predictors --- I didn't actually build this one, a user did).  In both
> cases you get a mixed of observed and latent discrete parameters, the
> latent ones of which can be marginalized out.
>
> Not to say it's easy.  We'd much rather have the marginalization be
> automatic and also to support explicit discrete parameters.
>
> I don't know the relation topic model.
>
> - Bob
>

Hi Vera,

I didn't try your second model. I'll take a look at it but it might be sometime before I have chance to do so since all my processors are currently running models.

Your first model did indeed take a bit of time on my server but there were are a quite a number of parameters so It wasn't that bad. That being said, to save some time you could try to run the chains in parallel instead of running them in series. Since you are still trying to improve the model you could also run only two chains at a time to save some time and run 4 chains when you'll have a more serious model.

You will also save some time if you use a more sensible number than 1e+05 for the inverse wishart prior. Unlike the other samplers Stan does try to explore the full parameter space and putting really large priors usually result in a really slow adaptive phase. However, if you take some time to browse the help list you'll see that many people don't like the use of the inverse-wishart distribution as a prior so maybe you could try something else.

Hope this help

Chris

messages.body_plain:
lp__ is just the value of the log of the total (parameters plus density)
probability density function less any constant normalizers.  The
sampling statements and increment_log_prob() statements both add to
lp__.

It is not restricted to be negative.

If you want help, please send your model and let us know
how you're initializing.

The problem you're having is with location, not with scale.

- Bob

messages.subject: fake frequentist statistics
messages.body_plain:
More a Bayesian than a stan question:

I have estimates of effects from models estimated with stan.  The PI is
very keen on (and is probably correct that the intended audience will be
keen) on getting p-values for effects, and also for questions like "do
the effects differ by race?"

How much justification is there for interpreting the posterior effect
estimates as frequentist estimate of the CI, and then doing frequentist
type tests on appropriate null hypotheses?  BDA 3rd edition indicates
this is generally asymptotically OK for parameter estimates, but these
are effect estimates.

Yes, I know point null hypotheses are kind of senseless from a Bayesian
perspective (as BDA also argues; some frequentists have also argued that
it's silly), and I am pushing for estimates of the probability that the
effect is "small" in some substantive sense.

Ross Boylan

> estimates as frequentist estimate of the CI, and then doing
> frequentist type tests on appropriate null hypotheses?  BDA 3rd
> edition indicates this is generally asymptotically OK for parameter
> estimates, but these are effect estimates.

One detail I suspect matters: the models are hierarchical and often have
low estimated variances for sets of parameters.  The same section that
says the equivalence is asymptotically OK says this is for
non-informative priors; I think the hierarchical model makes the priors
informative.

My fake chi-square test for equality of a set of 15 effects had p = 0.97
and another test of 15 different effects had p = 0.98; these seem
implausibly high, particularly given that the smallest simulated value
for the difference between the highest and lowest parameter exceeded
10%.  The single effect fake p-values (based on a normal approximation
with the mean and variance of the posterior) may not have been right,
but at least looked  plausible.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] fake frequentist statistics
messages.body_plain:
In general, no, posterior intervals will not have the correct frequentist coverage.  The asymptotic
limit where everything becomes a Gaussian and the intervals do have the correct coverage is
a subtle one and unlikely to be reached in practice (otherwise we wouldn’t need all of this heavy
statistical machinery in the first place).

If you wanted to be formal then the closest you could get would be to build up posterior predictive
distributions for any transformation of the parameters of interest and compute p-values there.  The
coverage won’t be correct because of the latent marginalization over parameters but it gives you
something you can at least attempt to understand from a frequentist perspective.

This also demonstrates why you’ll run into issues trying to estimate an overall effect — you’d need
a full joint distribution over the covariates in order to properly marginalize them out.  I believe
post-stratification is the right approach if you did want to push ahead here.

In the end the answer you need is a political one and not a statistical one...

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] convergence in stan
messages.body_plain:
You’ll want to focus your attention on the sigma_theta trace — everything stalls when
sigma_theta hits zero.  What’s happening here is that HMC (and just about everything)
is not geometrically ergodic for your model, and getting stuck like this is a manifestation
of the lack of geometric ergodicity.  You’ll also note that n_divergent becomes non-zero
in this region as well, which is an HMC specific manifestation of the problem.

This is particularly important as geometric ergodicity is what guarantees that Monte Carlo
estimates converge to the true expectations (via the Monte Carlo Central Limit Theorem),
and in a case like this you have to be very dubious of the estimates.  Note that algorithms
like Random Walk Metropolis and the Gibbs sampler suffer from the same problem, only
they’re usually not fast enough to be run for enough iterations to see the pathology manifest.

For more on the problem and possible solutions see http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906.

messages.body_plain:
On May 17, 2014, at 4:12 PM, Be <heart...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > I don't see how to compare any of these things given the wildly
> > multimodal posteriors you wind up getting.  It's not really possible
> > to do proper Bayesian inference in most of these models.
>
> I have an experience with comparing such models by reindexing topic indexes so that absolute difference minimizes.  I can say it works.
>

What are you comparing for?

If you compare the distributions across chains, you can often
get a few high-probability topics lining up fairly well.  But
then if you have K=50 in something like LDA, then only about
20 or 30 have lined up in my experience.  I think that's similar
to what Steyvers and Griffiths (2007) found:

  Steyvers, Mark and Tom Griffiths.
  2007.
  Probabilistic topic models.
  In Thomas K. Landauer, Danielle S. McNamara, Simon Dennis and
  Walter Kintsch (eds.), Handbook of Latent Semantic Analysis. Laurence Erlbaum.

See the section on "topic stability evaluation" in this tutorial I wrote for the last piece of software
I was working on before Stan (LingPipe) [which contains a full ref, too]:

  http://alias-i.com/lingpipe/demos/tutorial/cluster/read-me.html

That software follows Steyvers and Griffiths in going the other way,
marginalizing out the continuous parameters.

You can also find well-separated synthetic examples that line
up very well across chains with reindexing.  There's also an
example of that following Griffiths and Steyvers' example, too.

> > There are some results coming out using spectral methods about
> > separability in clusters and stability of inference, but I haven't
> > been keeping up with any of it and don't even know where to point you.
>
> I'm sorry.  I'd like to check mainly goodness of convergence and prediction performance (of some score Y).  I will use some toy data.
>

How do you want to measure convergence of a topic model like
this?  A single chain will converge pretty quickly, but even if
you take optimal index reassignment across chains, you won't see
very good convergence by measures like R-hat.

Other alternatives are using some kind of predictive evaluation,
like as a language model for new documents (which also requires
a marginalization, this time over topic distribution and topic
assignments).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Sat, 2014-05-17 at 13:01 +0100, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> In general, no, posterior intervals will not have the correct frequentist coverage.  The asymptotic
> limit where everything becomes a Gaussian and the intervals do have the correct coverage is
> a subtle one and unlikely to be reached in practice (otherwise we wouldn't need all of this heavy
> statistical machinery in the first place).
>
> If you wanted to be formal then the closest you could get would be to build up posterior predictive
> distributions for any transformation of the parameters of interest and compute p-values there.  The
> coverage won't be correct because of the latent marginalization over parameters but it gives you
> something you can at least attempt to understand from a frequentist perspective.
>

> This also demonstrates why you'll run into issues trying to estimate an overall effect -- you'd need

> a full joint distribution over the covariates in order to properly marginalize them out.  I believe
> post-stratification is the right approach if you did want to push ahead here.
>
> In the end the answer you need is a political one and not a statistical one...

Politically, there is a certain advantage to saying the requested
statistic is impossible to compute reliably.
Ross

>
> On May 16, 2014, at 8:03 PM, Ross Boylan <ro...@biostat.ucsf.edu> wrote:
>
> > More a Bayesian than a stan question:
> >
> > I have estimates of effects from models estimated with stan.  The PI is very keen on (and is probably correct that the intended audience will be keen) on getting p-values for effects, and also for questions like "do the effects differ by race?"
> >
> > How much justification is there for interpreting the posterior effect estimates as frequentist estimate of the CI, and then doing frequentist type tests on appropriate null hypotheses?  BDA 3rd edition indicates this is generally asymptotically OK for parameter estimates, but these are effect estimates.
> >
> > Yes, I know point null hypotheses are kind of senseless from a Bayesian perspective (as BDA also argues; some frequentists have also argued that it's silly), and I am pushing for estimates of the probability that the effect is "small" in some substantive sense.
