messages.subject: Extending a run
messages.body_plain:
I would like to write some code that automatically extends a chain.

I start with something like:
fit1 <- stan("MyModel.stan",data=my.data,
                  inits=my.inits,
                  chains=n.chains,iter=n.sample+n.warmup,
                  warmup=n.warmup)

suppose I now look at n_eff and I find that it is smaller than I want, so I define a new target length.
n_eff <- monitor(fit1,print=FALSE)[,"n_eff"]
newiter <- round(n.sample*min(max(1,n_eff.min/min(n_eff)),10))

where n_eff.min is the minimum acceptable value of n_eff.

So now I do a second run, something like:
  fit2 <- stan(fit=fit1,data=my.data,
                  inits=new.inits,
                  chains=n.chains,iter=newiter+n.warmup,
                  warmup=n.warmup)

I have several problems with this construction.
1) RStan doesn't seem to remember and reuse elements for the previous fit.  This doesn't work at all if I don't supply the data argument. If I leave off the number of chains, it returns to the RStan default of 4 (I prefer 3, but that is personal taste).  This behavior seems different from how other R functions like lm behave when starting from a previous fit.

2) It seems like RStan redoes the warmup.  This is a waste of time, as I was already happy with the previous warmup values.  It also produces a discontinuity if I try to paste the two results together. (see 4).

3) How do I set new.inits?  I could reuse my.inits, but I would prefer to start from where I left off.  The output of as.matrix seems ill suited to this purpose, as inits is looking for a list.

4) What I would really like to do is to combine the samples from fit1 and fit2 (as they are both ideally samples from the same posterior distribution).  For some purposes, I can just use rbind(as.matrix(fit1),as.matrix(fit2)), but for others I would like to keep this as a stanfit object so I can use the RStan methods.  Simply adding them in as new chains using sflist2stanfit won't work because the chains are of unequal length.

Thanks in advance for any advise you can give.

messages.subject: Re: How to marginalize latent variable z in supervised LDA?
messages.subject_clean: How to marginalize latent variable z in supervised LDA?
messages.body_plain:
It makes no sense to do LDA with Stan, except (maybe) for educational purposes.

I have lately used Wray Buntine's hca, available in mloss.org <http://mloss.org>. It can do basic LDA as well as more flexible priors. I have not done any quantitative comparisons, but the results are qualitatively, judged from topic "word" assignments, much better with hca than with the online LDA algorithm of Vowpal Wabbit. (Admittedly, I may be missing something important with the parameters of the VW, and the model is not the same, so the comparison is unfair.)

hca estimates by sampling, and the default models are with hierarchical "Pitman-Yor process" priors. (Calling it PYP is technically correct but a bit misleading , for the base measure is finite.)

Although collapsed Gibbs samplers of LDA-like models have no hope of sampling from the true posterior, they may still beat other methods in predictive performance, per CPU unit. Buntine has some comparisons related to this in his slides which I can't currently find by Google.

On May 20, 2014, at 2:42 PM, Janne Sinkkonen <janne.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

> It makes no sense to do LDA with Stan, except (maybe) for educational purposes.

I'd say the problem is MCMC, not Stan per se.  You can use Stan's
optimizers to fit LDA models with fixed priors.

The other reason to use something like Stan is for playing around
with different priors.

> I have lately used Wray Buntine's hca, available in mloss.org <http://mloss.org>. It can do basic LDA as well as more flexible priors. I have not done any quantitative comparisons, but the results are qualitatively, judged from topic "word" assignments, much better with hca than with the online LDA algorithm of Vowpal Wabbit. (Admittedly, I may be missing something important with the parameters of the VW, and the model is not the same, so the comparison is unfair.)

Matt Hoffman's algorithm in Vowpal Wabbit assumes you have a lot of
data.  Or presumably go through the data more than once.  I don't know
how VW's implemented there, but Matt obviously will :-)

We're working on generalizing the stochastic VB Matt did to Stan.
Maybe in another six months or a year we'll have something to release.

>
> hca estimates by sampling, and the default models are with hierarchical "Pitman-Yor process" priors. (Calling it PYP is technically correct but a bit misleading , for the base measure is finite.)

Is that something we could or should implement in Stan?

> Although collapsed Gibbs samplers of LDA-like models have no hope of sampling from the true posterior, they may still beat other methods in predictive performance, per CPU unit. Buntine has some comparisons related to this in his slides which I can't currently find by Google.

My own experience is that the inits matter a lot and the priors
on theta and beta matter a lot in terms of where you get to in the end.

My experience in industry is that customers love love love to see LDA output!
I like to present it a bit differently, by looking at something like TF/IDF
ranking of topics (for which I use z-scores) --- it works much better than
raw frequency to summarize topics (though I just pulled it out of thin
air --- there's no real motiviation). See:

http://alias-i.com/lingpipe/demos/tutorial/cluster/read-me.html

- Bob

You might want to leave a little leeway if you really need that minimum.

> 1) RStan doesn't seem to remember and reuse elements for the previous fit.  This doesn't work at all if I don't supply the data argument. If I leave off the number of chains, it returns to the RStan default of 4 (I prefer 3, but that is personal taste).  This behavior seems different from how other R functions like lm behave when starting from a previous fit.

Correct.  You need to pass it the last sample from the previous
fit as the init.  Then it'll have to go through warmup again, because
we aren't saving the warmup info in a way that we can read it back in.

Also, if you don't have enough effective samples, you sometimes need to
run warmup longer.  So we just suggest re-running from scratch with more
iterations (double is a good heuristic).

>
> 2) It seems like RStan redoes the warmup.  This is a waste of time, as I was already happy with the previous warmup values.  It also produces a discontinuity if I try to paste the two results together. (see 4).

That's the piece we need to add --- we don't have a way to say start
from the previous warmup values.  But it is on our short-term to-do list,
so we hope to get to it soon.

> 3) How do I set new.inits?  I could reuse my.inits, but I would prefer to start from where I left off.  The output of as.matrix seems ill suited to this purpose, as inits is looking for a list.

That's an R question I don't know the answer to.

>
> 4) What I would really like to do is to combine the samples from fit1 and fit2 (as they are both ideally samples from the same posterior distribution).  For some purposes, I can just use rbind(as.matrix(fit1),as.matrix(fit2)), but for others I would like to keep this as a stanfit object so I can use the RStan methods.  Simply adding them in as new chains using sflist2stanfit won't work because the chains are of unequal length.

You really need to concatenate them onto the end of the last chains.

Another issue on our refactoring the commands list is to deal with
R-hat and n_eff calculations with unequal chain sizes.  We don't right
now.  There are two obvious, but different ways to do this --- average
by chain or average by sample.    So this one's going to take some research.

- Bob

messages.subject: Lasso Coding - Error in Stan Manual?
messages.subject_clean: Lasso Coding - Error in Stan Manual?
messages.body_plain:
On page 353 in the Stan manual, there is some code for the Lasso.  The key line is:

increment_log_prob(lambda * abs(beta[k]));

However, lambda is always non-negative. Optimizing a model will maximize the log probability, so the above code produces larger beta values for larger lambda values.  The thinking behind Lasso is to produce smaller beta values for larger lambda.  I think what is really required is:

increment_log_prob( - lambda * abs(beta[k]));

Probably the same problem exists with the Ridge regression code and the elastic net code in the Stan manual.

Am I thinking about this correctly?

Thanks,
Howard

>
> As an LDA prior it may be clearly better than symmetric Dirichlet,

Well, we probably wouldn't use a symmetric Dirichlet in any
serious modeling we did (there was a Hannah Wallach paper on
why it's a bad idea for vanilla LDA, too, with demonstrations
of how a more informative prior for natural language could help).

> but  the (discrete) sampling scheme seems quite tricky.

We only get finitely many continuous parameters.  So we'd need
to marginalize out the discrete part.  I don't think that's
possible for Dirichlet processes, but I'm hardly a non-parametrics
algorithm expert (and if I'm wrong and someone can point me to how
to do it, that'd be super useful).

- Bob

On 5/17/2014 10:52 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> You’ll want to focus your attention on the sigma_theta trace — everything stalls when
> sigma_theta hits zero.  What’s happening here is that HMC (and just about everything)
> is not geometrically ergodic for your model, and getting stuck like this is a manifestation
> of the lack of geometric ergodicity.  You’ll also note that n_divergent becomes non-zero
> in this region as well, which is an HMC specific manifestation of the problem.
>
> This is particularly important as geometric ergodicity is what guarantees that Monte Carlo
> estimates converge to the true expectations (via the Monte Carlo Central Limit Theorem),
> and in a case like this you have to be very dubious of the estimates.  Note that algorithms
> like Random Walk Metropolis and the Gibbs sampler suffer from the same problem, only
> they’re usually not fast enough to be run for enough iterations to see the pathology manifest.
>
> For more on the problem and possible solutions see http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906.
>

Stan doesn't have support for any functions not in its manual.
This includes most of the R functions.

I have no idea what which.max does in R, but it's not in Stan.
Maybe someone who knows R can help you translate or you could
explain what you're trying to do.

You'll also find that Stan uses the "&&" notation for conjunction from
C++ (where "&" is bitwise and).

- Bob

On May 21, 2014, at 7:48 PM, retzerjj <retz...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
>
> On Friday, May 9, 2014 4:20:11 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> On May 8, 2014, at 5:47 AM, Retzer Joe <retz...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >> Your problem is here:
> >>
> >>> model {
> >>>  int rclass[N,D];
> >> ...
> >>>      rclass[i,j] ~ categorical(pi[i]);
> >>
> >> You don't ever set rclass.  The default value is 0, and then
> >> that causes a problem because 0 is not an appropriate outcome
> >> for a categorical.
> >>
> >
> > Right, we saw that with some print statements we had but removed before posting. We did try to limit / set the range with:
> >
> >      int<lower=1, upper=K> rclass[N,D];
> >   int<lower=1, upper=L> cclass[N,D];
>
> The problem isn't not setting the bounds, the problem is that you're
> trying to use "~" to do random number generation and assignment to
> rclass, and that's not how Stan works.  It requires rclass and pi to
> already be defined (not just declared as local variables) when you call
> it.  The parameters are all defined by default externally by the sampler,
> but any locals, transformed data, transformed parameters, and generated
> quantities need to be set explicitly before being used.
>
> >> It looks like what you're trying to do is sample from the
> >> categorical(pi[i]) and assign the result to rclass[i,j], which
> >> is NOT how Stan sampling statements work.  They just increment
> >> the log probability with the value of
> >>
> >>  log(Categorical(rclass[i,j] | pi[i]))
> >
> >
> > Yes, that is exactly what we are trying to do. I suspect our approach therefore is not correct. We would need to both set rclass (and cclass) appropriately and change our likelihood specification code, is that correct?
> >
>
> Correct.
>
> What you really need to do is marginalize out any discrete
> parameters.
>
> - Bob
>
> Thanks Bob. I tried re-writing to address the likelihood updating and to marginalize out the discrete parameters (using somewhat similar examples found on the list and the manual) and came up with the code below.
>
> my_code <- '
>  data {
>    int<lower=1> N;
>    int<lower=1> D;
>    int<lower=1> K;                // Number of row clusters
>    int<lower=1> L;                // Number of col clusters
>    int<lower=0,upper=1> x[N,D];
>    vector<lower=0>[K] alpha1;
>    vector<lower=0>[L] alpha2;
>  }
>
>  parameters {
>     real<lower=0,upper=1> theta[K,L];
>    //     real pi[N,K];
>    //     real pj[D,L];
>    simplex[K] pi[N];
>    simplex[L] pj[D];
>  }
>
>  model {
>    int rowSegVec[N];
>    int colSegVec[D];
>    real ps[N,D];
>    for(k in 1:K){                            # prior on theta - binomial prob for co-clusters
>      for(l in 1:L){theta[k,l] ~ beta(1, 1);}
>    }
>
>    for(i in 1:N) {                           # hierarchical prior on rows
>      pi[i] ~ dirichlet(alpha1);              # the individual class prob pi
>    }
>
>    for(j in 1:D) {                           # hierarchical prior on columns
>      pj[j] ~ dirichlet(alpha2);    # the individual class prob pj
>    }
>
>    for(i in 1:N){                             # likelihood
>      rowSegVec[i] ~ categorical(pi[i]);
>      for(j in 1:D){
>        colSegVec[j] ~ categorical(pj[j]);
>        for(l in 1:L){
>          for (k in 1:K){
>             if (which.max(rowSegVec[i])) == k &  which.max(colSegVec[j]) == l)
>                increment_log_prob(x[i,j]*log(Theta[k,l])+(1-x[i,j])*log1m(Theta[k,l]));
>            }
>          }
>        }
>      }
>    }
>  '
> I'm now running into the error:

> It would seem the R "which.max" function is not recognized by stan, though there could be other problems. I was wondering if there was an equivalent function in R and/or if there might be any additional obvious problems with the code re-write.

messages.body_plain:
which.max <http://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/which.min.html> in R cycles through a vector and returns the index with the largest value. To do that in Stan, you'll probably have to write an extra loop and store the value. One observation, though. RowSegVec is a vector, so RowSegVec[i] is a single observation, which.max shouldn't apply, unless I missed something.

--Avi

On Wednesday, May 21, 2014 8:31:25 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Stan doesn't have support for any functions not in its manual.
> This includes most of the R functions.
>
> I have no idea what which.max does in R, but it's not in Stan.
> Maybe someone who knows R can help you translate or you could
> explain what you're trying to do.
>
> You'll also find that Stan uses the "&&" notation for conjunction from
> C++ (where "&" is bitwise and).
>
> - Bob
>
> On May 21, 2014, at 7:48 PM, retzerjj <retz...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> >
> >
> > On Friday, May 9, 2014 4:20:11 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > On May 8, 2014, at 5:47 AM, Retzer Joe <retz...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > >> Your problem is here:
> > >>
> > >>> model {
> > >>>  int rclass[N,D];
> > >> ...
> > >>>      rclass[i,j] ~ categorical(pi[i]);
> > >>
> > >> You don't ever set rclass.  The default value is 0, and then
> > >> that causes a problem because 0 is not an appropriate outcome
> > >> for a categorical.
> > >>
> > >
> > > Right, we saw that with some print statements we had but removed before posting. We did try to limit / set the range with:
> > >
> > >      int<lower=1, upper=K> rclass[N,D];
> > >   int<lower=1, upper=L> cclass[N,D];
> >
> > The problem isn't not setting the bounds, the problem is that you're
> > trying to use "~" to do random number generation and assignment to
> > rclass, and that's not how Stan works.  It requires rclass and pi to
> > already be defined (not just declared as local variables) when you call
> > it.  The parameters are all defined by default externally by the sampler,
> > but any locals, transformed data, transformed parameters, and generated
> > quantities need to be set explicitly before being used.
> >
> > >> It looks like what you're trying to do is sample from the
> > >> categorical(pi[i]) and assign the result to rclass[i,j], which
> > >> is NOT how Stan sampling statements work.  They just increment
> > >> the log probability with the value of
> > >>
> > >>  log(Categorical(rclass[i,j] | pi[i]))
> > >
> > >
> > > Yes, that is exactly what we are trying to do. I suspect our approach therefore is not correct. We would need to both set rclass (and cclass) appropriately and change our likelihood specification code, is that correct?
> > >
> >
> > Correct.
> >
> > What you really need to do is marginalize out any discrete
> > parameters.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > Thanks Bob. I tried re-writing to address the likelihood updating and to marginalize out the discrete parameters (using somewhat similar examples found on the list and the manual) and came up with the code below.
> >
> > my_code <- '
> >  data {
> >    int<lower=1> N;
> >    int<lower=1> D;
> >    int<lower=1> K;                // Number of row clusters
> >    int<lower=1> L;                // Number of col clusters
> >    int<lower=0,upper=1> x[N,D];
> >    vector<lower=0>[K] alpha1;
> >    vector<lower=0>[L] alpha2;
> >  }
> >
> >  parameters {
> >     real<lower=0,upper=1> theta[K,L];
> >    //     real pi[N,K];
> >    //     real pj[D,L];
> >    simplex[K] pi[N];
> >    simplex[L] pj[D];
> >  }
> >
> >  model {
> >    int rowSegVec[N];
> >    int colSegVec[D];
> >    real ps[N,D];
> >    for(k in 1:K){                            # prior on theta - binomial prob for co-clusters
> >      for(l in 1:L){theta[k,l] ~ beta(1, 1);}
> >    }
> >
> >    for(i in 1:N) {                           # hierarchical prior on rows
> >      pi[i] ~ dirichlet(alpha1);              # the individual class prob pi
> >    }
> >
> >    for(j in 1:D) {                           # hierarchical prior on columns
> >      pj[j] ~ dirichlet(alpha2);    # the individual class prob pj
> >    }
> >
> >    for(i in 1:N){                             # likelihood
> >      rowSegVec[i] ~ categorical(pi[i]);
> >      for(j in 1:D){
> >        colSegVec[j] ~ categorical(pj[j]);
> >        for(l in 1:L){
> >          for (k in 1:K){
> >             if (which.max(rowSegVec[i])) == k &  which.max(colSegVec[j]) == l)
> >                increment_log_prob(x[i,j]*log(Theta[k,l])+(1-x[i,j])*log1m(Theta[k,l]));
> >            }
> >          }
> >        }
> >      }
> >    }
> >  '
> > I'm now running into the error:
> >
> > TRANSLATING MODEL 'my_code' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
> > Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
> >   failed to parse Stan model 'my_code' with error message:
> > EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=42, column=40
> >
> >             if (which.max(rowSegVec[i])) == k &  which.max(colSegVec[j]) == l)
> >                                        ^-- here
> >
> >
> > DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> > no matches for function name="which.max"
> >     arg 0 type=int
> > available function signatures for which.max:
> > expression is ill formed

> >
> > You'll also find that Stan uses the "&&" notation for conjunction from
> > C++ (where "&" is bitwise and).
> >
> > - Bob

> > On May 21, 2014, at 7:48 PM, retzerjj <retz...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > >
> > >

> > >
> > > On May 8, 2014, at 5:47 AM, Retzer Joe <retz...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > >> Your problem is here:
> > > >>
> > > >>> model {
> > > >>>  int rclass[N,D];
> > > >> ...
> > > >>>      rclass[i,j] ~ categorical(pi[i]);
> > > >>
> > > >> You don't ever set rclass.  The default value is 0, and then
> > > >> that causes a problem because 0 is not an appropriate outcome
> > > >> for a categorical.
> > > >>
> > > >
> > > > Right, we saw that with some print statements we had but removed before posting. We did try to limit / set the range with:
> > > >
> > > >      int<lower=1, upper=K> rclass[N,D];
> > > >   int<lower=1, upper=L> cclass[N,D];
> > >
> > > The problem isn't not setting the bounds, the problem is that you're
> > > trying to use "~" to do random number generation and assignment to
> > > rclass, and that's not how Stan works.  It requires rclass and pi to
> > > already be defined (not just declared as local variables) when you call
> > > it.  The parameters are all defined by default externally by the sampler,
> > > but any locals, transformed data, transformed parameters, and generated
> > > quantities need to be set explicitly before being used.
> > >
> > > >> It looks like what you're trying to do is sample from the
> > > >> categorical(pi[i]) and assign the result to rclass[i,j], which
> > > >> is NOT how Stan sampling statements work.  They just increment
> > > >> the log probability with the value of
> > > >>
> > > >>  log(Categorical(rclass[i,j] | pi[i]))
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Yes, that is exactly what we are trying to do. I suspect our approach therefore is not correct. We would need to both set rclass (and cclass) appropriately and change our likelihood specification code, is that correct?
> > > >
> > >
> > > Correct.
> > >
> > > What you really need to do is marginalize out any discrete
> > > parameters.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >

> > >    int<lower=1> D;
> > >    int<lower=1> K;                // Number of row clusters

> > >    int<lower=0,upper=1> x[N,D];
> > >    vector<lower=0>[K] alpha1;
> > >    vector<lower=0>[L] alpha2;
> > >  }
> > >
> > >  parameters {
> > >     real<lower=0,upper=1> theta[K,L];
> > >    //     real pi[N,K];
> > >    //     real pj[D,L];
> > >    simplex[K] pi[N];
> > >    simplex[L] pj[D];
> > >  }
> > >
> > >  model {
> > >    int rowSegVec[N];
> > >    int colSegVec[D];
> > >    real ps[N,D];
> > >    for(k in 1:K){                            # prior on theta - binomial prob for co-clusters
> > >      for(l in 1:L){theta[k,l] ~ beta(1, 1);}
> > >    }
> > >
> > >    for(i in 1:N) {                           # hierarchical prior on rows
> > >      pi[i] ~ dirichlet(alpha1);              # the individual class prob pi
> > >    }
> > >
> > >    for(j in 1:D) {                           # hierarchical prior on columns
> > >      pj[j] ~ dirichlet(alpha2);    # the individual class prob pj
> > >    }
> > >
> > >    for(i in 1:N){                             # likelihood
> > >      rowSegVec[i] ~ categorical(pi[i]);
> > >      for(j in 1:D){
> > >        colSegVec[j] ~ categorical(pj[j]);
> > >        for(l in 1:L){
> > >          for (k in 1:K){
> > >             if (which.max(rowSegVec[i])) == k &  which.max(colSegVec[j]) == l)
> > >                increment_log_prob(x[i,j]*log(Theta[k,l])+(1-x[i,j])*log1m(Theta[k,l]));
> > >            }
> > >          }
> > >        }
> > >      }
> > >    }
> > >  '

Hi,

One needs to use the same compiler for Python as for PyStan. Perhaps Python was
compiled with g++ and you're using clang (even if it is clang masquerading as
g++).

I've created a stub of a page to collect OS X related problems and solutions here:
https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan/wiki/PyStan-and-OS-X-Mavericks Let us know if
the suggested solution works for you.

Best wishes,

-a

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] error multi_normal
messages.body_plain:
The problem is that the first argument needs to be a vector, not
a row vector.  Here's the relevant part of the error message:

> TRANSLATING MODEL 'mod' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
> Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
>   failed to parse Stan model 'mod' with error message:
> EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=23, column=37
>
> phi[1] ~ multi_normal( mu0p , C0p );
>                                     ^-- here
>
>

>     arg 0 type=row vector
>     arg 1 type=vector
>     arg 2 type=matrix
> available function signatures for multi_normal_log:
> 0.  multi_normal_log(vector, vector, matrix) : real

The first part says that you called multi_normal with phi[1] a row_vector,
mu0p a vector, and c0p a matrix.

The second part says the only argument pattern support is (vector, vector, matrix).

The easy solution is to transpose phi[1]:

  phi[1]' ~ multi_normal( mu0p , C0p );

A more efficient approach is to declare phi
as an array of vectors:

  vector[N] phi[T];

Then you can use your original version and there's
no copying required anywhere internally.  There's a manual chapter up
front discussing the differences between arrays and matrices and
their efficiencies and restrictions.

- Bob

Looking for folks encountering similar problems with Numpy and Scipy is a good
strategy for finding solutions for this kind of issue.

It seems like paying attention to compiler consistency on OS X has worked well
for people. For example, if one is going to use clang then make sure everything
is using clang.

If it helps, it's possible to identify the compiler used to compile Python just
by launching it. If you type "python" in the terminal the second line will tell
you the precise version of the compiler that was used.

Good luck!

-a

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] error multi_normal
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sharing the data.

I'm afraid I don't have any suggestions for a workaround.

We're working on our error checking tolerances, which
are also causing failures in high-dimensional correlation
matrices.  These both use Cholesky factors as unconstrained
representations, but I'd have expected the covariance matrix
decomposition to be pretty stable.

The issue is arithmetic, not mathematical.  That is, if
we were operating on real numbers, we wouldn't have this
problem.  Big matrix operations and exponentiation (to keep
the Cholesky factor's diagonal positive) on floating point is a whole
different business.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Binomial hierarchical model
messages.body_plain:
On May 25, 2014, at 4:10 PM, pehl...@gmail.com wrote:

>
> I am trying to analyse a toy example that I have created in R.
>
> We can imagine the example as follows: we have followed 12 populations and measured a certain illness in the population. We are interested in the probability of being ill.
>
> Now we divide these populations in males and females which have their own probabilities in turn (we could in theory slice and dice the data differently).

What'll happen in general is that we'll do a logistic regression, not directly
estimate probabilities for subpopulations.

> I would have intuitively expected that if a population is small its probability should be closer to the total population probability and vice versa. So this is why I believe a hierarchical model might be useful.

You mean you want to partially pool the male and female populations
using a hierarchical model?  That you can do.

> I have coded such a model in stan, but I have some convergence issues. I would like to understand if my approach is appropriate and if so how I can modify my code so that it converges.
>
> I have generated my data as follows:
>
> library(rstan)
> set_cppo('fast')
>
> set.seed(123)
> population  <- rbinom(12,140,seq(0.1,0.9,length.out=12))
> sick <- rbinom(12,population,0.01)
>
> male <- rbinom(12,population,0.8)
> female <- population - male
> sick2 <- rbinom(12,sick,0.6)
> sick1 <- sick - sick2
>
> dat <- list(noexp=12,
>             sub=3,
>             pop = c(population,male,female),
>             sick = c(sick,sick1,sick2),
>             popind = rep(1:3,each=12))
>
> fit <- stan(file="binom.stan",data=dat,iter=10000,chains=3,thin=10)

The trick is now to just write the model to match your
simulation, which your model below doesn't quite do.  It
helps (me at least) to use the same variables in the
simulation as in the model, so they're easy to line up and
test for fit against the posterior.

>
> To analyse the data I have used the following model.
>
> data {
>   int noexp;              // number of experiments
>   int sub;                // number of subpop
>   int pop[sub*noexp];     // populations
>   int sick[sub*noexp];    // sick
>   int popind[sub*noexp];  // pop index
> }
>

These all seem to be declared with the wrong
sizes given the way you loop over only parts of them below.

> parameters {
>   real<lower=0> tau;
>   real eta[sub];
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real psick[sub];
>   psick[1] <- inv_logit(100*eta[1]);
>   for (j in 2:sub)
>     psick[j] <- inv_logit(logit(psick[1]) + tau*eta[j]);
> }
>

I don't understand why these all involve a psick[1] term.

> model {
>   eta ~ normal(0,1);
>   for (i in 1:noexp)
>     sick[i] ~ binomial(pop[i],psick[popind[i]]);
> }

At this point, you just want to declare some parameters and
use a logit scaled predictor as the chance of success in
a call to binomial_logit().  That is, don't do your own inv_logit
transform --- it should just look like this:

   sick[i] ~ binomial_logit(pop[i], logit(psick[1]) + tau*eta[j]);

Anyway, the usual way to do this would be to just write a hierarchical
logistic regression, which is here intercept-only because you don't have
other predictors in your simulation other than the population index
if I understand correctly.

- Bob

Downgrading R is never really the answer. It is just a matter of getting everything aligned. The first thing to try seems to be reinstalling Rcpp from source with

install.packages(c("Rcpp", "inline"), type = "source")

If that is insufficient to get rstan working, then should do a

remove.packages("rstan")

and then install rstan again. If you are using the latest version of the Mac operating system, then I think you have to install rstan with CXX=g++ in ~/.R/Makevars and then change it to CXX=clang++ when you want to run models.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] error multi_normal
messages.body_plain:
Given that all of the covariance matrices you use are
declared as parameters, I think this is a bug on our
side with validating the positive definiteness too strictly.

To debug, I'd start by trying to figure out which instance is
causing the problem.  You can comment all the multi_normal out and
then reintroduce them one by one (with all others commented
out) to isolate the issue.

One problem you might have is that only sigma and omega
have priors --- this shouldn't be an issue with init, though.

It's too bad we don't do a better job of isolating the line throwing
the error in Stan --- we only tell you the type of distribution, not which
particular instance.  We have some vague plans to try to fix this
in the future, but it's a surprisingly huge amount of work
(though I'm sure eventually worth the investment if we can do
it without too much of a slowdown in most cases).

- Bob

messages.subject: Simple Multivariate Normal Question
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have what I think is a relatively simple question about modeling multivariate normal data.  My data consists of N independent d-dimensional multivariate normals, (assume d is small, like 2, but N possibly large).  They all have the same covariance but different means.

What is the best way to implement this efficiently, with vectorization?  Since N is large I want to do this as efficiently as possible.

Should I represent my data as an N x 2 matrix, and then doing something like

for(idx in 1:N){
      y[idx,] ~ multi_normal(mu[idx,],Sigma)
}

I had read that the sampling statements in loops are relatively slow, so I was thinking there should be a way to represent this using some sort of reparameterization:

z ~ normal(0,1)
y <- mu+L*z

where z is a Nx2matrix as well, but its not clear to me that this is possible when y is data and not a transformed parameter.

Also, mu is of much smaller effective dimension than N (like in regression), so I'd prefer not to represent mu as a transformed parameter.  I think my problem is somewhat similar to the multivariate regression example in the manual, but my outcome is multivariate as well.

Thanks for any insight!

messages.subject: variability of an effect
messages.body_plain:
I have estimates of the distribution of an effect across K groups, where
K is small, like 3.  The overall goal is to get an estimate of the the
variability of the effect across groups.  For each set of coefficients,
call it B_j for the j'th set, g_kj is the group effect for the k'th group.

One can compute the variance of g across k for each j, and have a
posterior distribution for the variance.

Should the individual variances use K or K-1 as the divisor?  If B_j
actually were the correct coefficients it seems to me K would be more
appropriate--although I suppose even in that case we are still
estimating g_kj since we only have a sample of the target population k.

I'm also planning on using the range of the g_kj across k as a measure
of dispersion.

It's possible the whole strategy is misconceived; if so, let me know :)

I have managed to convince my colleagues that test of the null
hypothesis that all effects are equal is neither possible nor desirable
(or at least, that it's not possible).  These other measures are an
effort to come up with a more useful, and more Bayesian, alternative.

These are estimates of variability of effects, not of variability in the
original model parameters, and so there is no variance parameter in a
hierarchical model that corresponds to the effects.

One other wrinkle is that the group effects are themselves aggregations
of individual effects.  So we start with estimates of the individual
effects, d_ij, for individual i under coefficient set j.  g_kj is the
mean of the d_ij for  the subset of i in group k.

messages.body_plain:
On May 30, 2014, at 8:03 PM, Ross Boylan <ro...@biostat.ucsf.edu> wrote:

> I have estimates of the distribution of an effect across K groups, where K is small, like 3.  The overall goal is to get an estimate of the the variability of the effect across groups.  For each set of coefficients, call it B_j for the j'th set, g_kj is the group effect for the k'th group.
>
> One can compute the variance of g across k for each j, and have a posterior distribution for the variance.
>
> Should the individual variances use K or K-1 as the divisor?

> If B_j actually were the correct coefficients it seems to me K would be more appropriate--although I suppose even in that case we are still estimating g_kj since we only have a sample of the target population k.

The point would be to assume the K you observe are part of
some larger population you're trying to estimate.  In
that case, 1/K yields the maximum likelihood estimator and 1/(K-1)
an unbiased estimator.

I would think the variance across groups would be very sensitive
to the priors you're using unless there's a lot of data per group.

> I'm also planning on using the range of the g_kj across k as a measure of dispersion.

Tail measures like 95% intervals are hard to estimate and require many more
samples.

>
> It's possible the whole strategy is misconceived; if so, let me know :)

I see you mention below you can't do a hierarchical model.  I didn't
understand why.  That'd be the usual approach, and then you can read off
the variance from there and it'll also determine the amount of pooling.

> I have managed to convince my colleagues that test of the null hypothesis that all effects are equal is neither possible nor desirable (or at least, that it's not possible).

It's not possible from a Bayesian perspective, because that's
a measure-zero event.  You can measure usual event probabilities
like Pr(theta[1] > theta[2]) and the like.

Again, I'm not sure why you're not setting up a hierarchical model.

The prior variance is going to determine how much pooling
you do (all effects are equal is complete pooling, each
estimated independently is no pooling, which is presumably what
you're doing).

> These other measures are an effort to come up with a more useful, and more Bayesian, alternative.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] variability of an effect
messages.body_plain:
On 5/30/2014 11:28 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On May 30, 2014, at 8:03 PM, Ross Boylan <ro...@biostat.ucsf.edu> wrote:
>
>> I have estimates of the distribution of an effect across K groups, where K is small, like 3.  The overall goal is to get an estimate of the the variability of the effect across groups.  For each set of coefficients, call it B_j for the j'th set, g_kj is the group effect for the k'th group.
>>
>> One can compute the variance of g across k for each j, and have a posterior distribution for the variance.
>>
>> Should the individual variances use K or K-1 as the divisor?
>> If B_j actually were the correct coefficients it seems to me K would be more appropriate--although I suppose even in that case we are still estimating g_kj since we only have a sample of the target population k.
> The point would be to assume the K you observe are part of
> some larger population you're trying to estimate.  In
> that case, 1/K yields the maximum likelihood estimator and 1/(K-1)
> an unbiased estimator.

The categories here are ethnic groups.  Taking them (the categories, not
the individuals in them) as part of a larger population of categories
seems unnatural.  The division into 3 includes most groups (whites being
the notable exception), and there is another division into 5 racial
categories that completely partitions the space ("other" is one of the 5
categories).  The 3 categories are a subset of the 5 categories, and so
are part of a slightly larger (but far from infinite) population.  But
the 5 aren't part of anything larger.

The racial/ethnic groups are themselves social constructs, and the
degree of refinement---saying that there is a group that is Latino as
opposed to separate groups for each country or separate groups for
Latino based on skin color---it itself an analytic decision rather than
a feature of nature.

>
> I would think the variance across groups would be very sensitive
> to the priors you're using unless there's a lot of data per group.

If you mean observed data, we have several hundred per ethnic group.

>> I'm also planning on using the range of the g_kj across k as a measure of dispersion.
> Tail measures like 95% intervals are hard to estimate and require many more
> samples.

The range doesn't seem much like a tail measure, at least if K is low.
The g are already averages, and I would think the distribution of
differences between them has more to do with the fat part of the
distributions.  We do have some situation with 15 (3x5) categories, and
the maximum difference statistic seems more problematic there.

Concretely, suppose we knew that African-American (AA) respondents with
Asian/Pacific Islander (API) partners had a 50% chance of having risky
sex and all 14 other combinations had a 30% chance of risky sex.  The
variance of the respondent x partner interaction is modest in this case,
and if we did a frequentist test for the equality of all effects it
would likely come out with "data consistent with the null" for samples
that weren't too big.  Despite low variance and unimpressive p, I would
consider the interaction important in this case.  That's the kind of
thing I'm trying to capture with the range statistic.

>
>> It's possible the whole strategy is misconceived; if so, let me know :)
> I see you mention below you can't do a hierarchical model.  I didn't
> understand why.  That'd be the usual approach, and then you can read off
> the variance from there and it'll also determine the amount of pooling.

The effect estimates are the results of simulations that use
hierarchical models.  The input models are hierarchical, but the output
effect estimates are a result of a complicated transformation of those
inputs.  The effect estimates are model outputs, not data inputs.

Are you suggesting treating the draws from the  posterior as "data"
inputs to a hierarchical model?

What I meant, more precisely, is that the hierarchical models I have are
not directly models of effects, and so the variance parameters in them
do not translate directly to the variance of effects.

>
>> I have managed to convince my colleagues that test of the null hypothesis that all effects are equal is neither possible nor desirable (or at least, that it's not possible).
> It's not possible from a Bayesian perspective, because that's
> a measure-zero event.  You can measure usual event probabilities
> like Pr(theta[1] > theta[2]) and the like.
>
>
> Again, I'm not sure why you're not setting up a hierarchical model.
>
> The prior variance is going to determine how much pooling
> you do (all effects are equal is complete pooling, each
> estimated independently is no pooling, which is presumably what
> you're doing).
>
>> These other measures are an effort to come up with a more useful, and more Bayesian, alternative.
>> These are estimates of variability of effects, not of variability in the original model parameters, and so there is no variance parameter in a hierarchical model that corresponds to the effects.
> What is the prior on the parameters you're using?

The input models have lots of terms that are interactions between the
categories (respondent race) and covariates.  Typically the individual
parameter estimates were from a model in which they had a normal(0,
sigma) distribution with sigma~cauchy(0, 5).  Different degrees of
interaction had different sigmas.  The effects are the result of all the
interactions (in all relevant models) and the distribution of the input
covariates.

>
>> One other wrinkle is that the group effects are themselves aggregations of individual effects.  So we start with estimates of the individual effects, d_ij, for individual i under coefficient set j.  g_kj is the mean of the d_ij for  the subset of i in group k.
> You mean g is literally calculated as a data mean?

It is the mean of the individual simulated effects.  I wouldn't call the
effects data.  The effect estimates for individuals, d_ij, are
themselves estimates of the mean effect for that individual, rather than
simply differences in simulated outcomes.  For example, in estimating an
effect on a binary outcome, d_ij is the expected change in the
probability of the outcome between two scenarios given by an
intervention for individual i.

Ross
